stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever and a productive cough of yellowish sputum. Medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus. He is a smoker. His chest examination reveals decreased breath sounds throughout and crackles at the right lung base. Other systemic examination is unremarkable (see report). Chest radiograph: Right lower lobe infiltrate. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptA: Admit him, start ceftriaxone and azithromycin
OptD: Outpatient treatment with cefuroxime and azithromycin
why_right: This is community-acquired pneumonia (fever, purulent sputum, "right lower lobe infiltrate") in a 45-year-old with no confusion, no reported shock or respiratory failure, so CURB-65 is 0 and outpatient care is appropriate. Because he has a comorbidity ("type 2 diabetes mellitus"), outpatient therapy is a beta-lactam (cefuroxime) plus a macrolide (azithromycin) rather than a macrolide alone.
why_wrong_block:
A. Admit and start ceftriaxone plus azithromycin: the correct regimen for an inpatient (ward) CAP, but this patient has a low severity score and does not need admission.
B. Admit and start IV amoxicillin: wrong setting (no admission needed) and it lacks atypical cover.
C. Outpatient azithromycin alone: monotherapy is for previously healthy outpatients without comorbidities (and only where macrolide resistance is low); diabetes requires combination therapy.
key_concept:
CAP: decide the setting by CURB-65, then the regimen by comorbidity.
  • CURB-65: Confusion, Urea raised, RR ≥ 30, low BP, age ≥ 65
  • Score 0 to 1: outpatient
  • Healthy outpatient: amoxicillin or a macrolide/doxycycline
  • Outpatient with comorbidity (diabetes, heart, lung, liver, kidney disease): beta-lactam plus macrolide, or respiratory fluoroquinolone
  • Inpatient ward: ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
exam_pearl: Diabetes does not mean admission; it only upgrades the outpatient regimen to combination therapy.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: D highlighted with 'D✔️ Gameboy'. Screenshot in the same block (next page; version with D = cefuroxime, No Azithromycin): Alhomrani & Naif-SMLE Elite: A. Admit him, start ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Diabetic OR smoker = needs beta-lactam AND azithromycin.
Other marked answers: Alhomrani & Naif-SMLE Elite (screenshot): A

stem: 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever and a productive cough of yellowish sputum. Medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus. He is a smoker. His chest examination reveals decreased breath sounds throughout and crackles at the right lung base. Other systemic examination is unremarkable (see report). Chest radiograph: Right lower lobe infiltrate. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Fever, productive yellow sputum, right basal crackles and a right lower lobe infiltrate are community acquired pneumonia. The standard empirical regimen is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin: the beta lactam covers typical organisms such as pneumococcus and H. influenzae, and the macrolide covers atypicals. Diabetes is a comorbidity that calls for beta lactam plus macrolide rather than a macrolide alone, but neither it nor smoking is a risk factor for MRSA or Pseudomonas.
why_wrong_block:
B. Vancomycin is added only with MRSA risk factors (prior MRSA, recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics, necrotizing or cavitary pneumonia), and it gives no gram negative cover.
C. An antiviral such as oseltamivir is for influenza (season, myalgia, positive test); a lobar infiltrate with purulent sputum is bacterial.
D. One source keyed meropenem, but it is for hospital acquired pneumonia or Pseudomonas or resistant gram negative risk (recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics, prior Pseudomonas, structural lung disease); none is present, so it is unnecessarily broad for this CAP.
key_concept:
Empirical CAP therapy depends on severity and risk factors.
  • Healthy outpatient: macrolide or doxycycline
  • Outpatient with comorbidity (e.g. diabetes): beta lactam plus macrolide, or respiratory fluoroquinolone
  • Ward inpatient: ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
  • MRSA risk: add vancomycin or linezolid
  • Pseudomonas risk or HAP: antipseudomonal agent (piperacillin tazobactam, meropenem)
exam_pearl: If the options include outpatient care with CURB-65 of 0, an oral beta lactam plus macrolide at home becomes the answer for this same patient.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Second version (Q) under 578 with a different option set. Supporting screenshot (Q 0195: 42-year-old with productive cough, fever, dyspnea, right lower lung consolidation; empiric regimen): Answer: B = Ceftriaxone and azithromycin. A 'D✅Gameboy' line follows this block.
Other marked answers: Gameboy: D

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever and a productive cough of yellowish sputum. Medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus. He is a smoker. His chest examination reveals decreased breath sounds throughout and crackles at the right lung base. Other systemic examination is unremarkable (see report). Chest radiograph: Right lower lobe infiltrate. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptA: Admit him, start ceftriaxone and azithromycin
why_right: This recall's key is outpatient cefuroxime. The decisive clues are an otherwise stable 45-year-old ("other systemic examination is unremarkable") with a single-lobe infiltrate, so CURB-65 is 0 and he can be treated at home. Because he has a comorbidity (type 2 diabetes, plus smoking), he should not get macrolide monotherapy; he needs a beta-lactam such as cefuroxime as the backbone. Note that the same scenario elsewhere is keyed to cefuroxime plus azithromycin, which is the guideline regimen.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the correct regimen for a patient who needs admission (ward CAP), but with CURB-65 of 0 this stable man does not need to be admitted.
B. Admission is not indicated at CURB-65 0, and IV amoxicillin alone gives no atypical cover.
C. Azithromycin monotherapy is reserved for healthy outpatients without comorbidities; diabetes (and smoking) calls for beta-lactam based therapy instead.
key_concept:
CAP: CURB-65 decides WHERE, comorbidity decides WHAT.
  • CURB-65: Confusion, Urea >7, RR ≥30, BP low (SBP <90 or DBP ≤60), age ≥65
  • Score 0 to 1: outpatient; 2: consider admission; ≥3: admit, consider ICU
  • Healthy outpatient: macrolide (azithromycin) or doxycycline alone
  • Outpatient with comorbidity (DM, heart, lung, liver, renal disease): beta-lactam (amoxicillin-clavulanate or cefuroxime) PLUS macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone
  • Inpatient ward: ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
exam_pearl: Diabetes changes the drug, not the site of care: a stable diabetic with CURB-65 0 still goes home.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Note: a screenshot of this same option set appears just above (in 578's block) marked by Alhomrani & Naif-SMLE Elite as A (diabetic or smoker = beta-lactam AND azithromycin).

stem: 13- years old female presented with chronic diarrhoea and altered bowel habits for 3-4 months, did colonoscopy: showed transmural inflamed patches, what is the first-option treatment?
why_right: Chronic diarrhoea for months with "transmural inflamed patches" (skip lesions, full thickness inflammation) is Crohn's disease. To induce remission of active luminal disease, systemic corticosteroids are the classic first option among these choices; they act quickly but are not used for maintenance.
why_wrong_block:
B. Infliximab (anti-TNF) is for fistulizing or perianal disease, severe or high-risk disease, or steroid refractory/dependent cases, not the routine first option for uncomplicated luminal Crohn's.
C. Methotrexate is a steroid-sparing maintenance agent; it is slow in onset and not used to induce remission first.
D. This is a placeholder from the recaller, not a treatment option.
key_concept:
Crohn's disease: induce, then maintain.
  • Transmural, patchy (skip) inflammation, often terminal ileum: Crohn's
  • Induction, pediatric: exclusive enteral nutrition or corticosteroids
  • Maintenance: azathioprine or methotrexate
  • Fistulizing/perianal or severe disease: anti-TNF (infliximab)
  • Steroids never for maintenance
exam_pearl: If "exclusive enteral nutrition" or "manage nutrition" is offered in a child with luminal Crohn's, it is the preferred first-line induction over steroids.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q): patient complaining of abdominal (pain); microscopic finding transmural patchy at terminal ileum (diagnosis not written); management: manage nutrition / methotrexate / infliximab / steroid (no mark).

stem: A full-term infant of a diabetic mother has a hematocrit of 71% and appears plethoric. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: An infant of a diabetic mother with a hematocrit of 71% and plethora has neonatal polycythemia (venous hematocrit above 65%). The stem gives no symptoms of hyperviscosity (no lethargy, respiratory distress, hypoglycaemia or seizures), so management is hydration with IV fluids and monitoring; partial exchange is kept for symptomatic infants.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance alone ignores a hematocrit well above the polycythemia threshold; the baby needs hydration and monitoring for hyperviscosity complications.
B. Partial exchange transfusion with saline is for symptomatic polycythemia (hyperviscosity signs) or very high hematocrits; plethora alone is a sign of polycythemia, not a hyperviscosity symptom.
C. Phototherapy treats hyperbilirubinemia; polycythemia raises the jaundice risk, but there is no jaundice here and it does not lower the hematocrit.
key_concept:
Neonatal polycythemia: venous hematocrit above 65%.
  • Causes: infant of diabetic mother, IUGR, delayed cord clamping, twin to twin transfusion
  • Signs: plethora, lethargy, poor feeding, respiratory distress, hypoglycaemia, jaundice
  • Asymptomatic: IV fluids/hydration and monitoring
  • Symptomatic (hyperviscosity): partial exchange transfusion
  • Always check glucose in an IDM
exam_pearl: Plethora is not a symptom; if the stem adds lethargy, seizures, respiratory distress or hypoglycaemia, the answer flips to partial exchange transfusion.

stem: An Elderly Man (60–70 Years) With Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension, BMI 31, And A History Of Smoking (Stopped 15 Years Ago) Presents With Difficulty Walking Short Distances. What Is The Primary Risk Factor For His Symptoms?
OptC: It Is Normal For His Age
why_right: Trouble walking short distances in an older patient with vascular risk factors points to intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease. This recall's key is hypertension and obesity because they are his current, active risk factors, whereas he stopped smoking 15 years ago. The question is testing that symptoms come from atherosclerosis driven by ongoing modifiable risk factors, not from ageing.
why_wrong_block:
A. Smoking is the strongest single risk factor for PAD in active smokers, but he quit 15 years ago, which the recall uses to make it a historical rather than current driver. It would be the answer if he were still smoking.
C. Reduced walking distance is not normal ageing; exertional limb symptoms with multiple vascular risk factors need assessment for PAD (ankle-brachial index).
key_concept:
Claudication = PAD until proven otherwise.
  • Major PAD risk factors: smoking (strongest), diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, age
  • Obesity adds risk mainly through HTN, DM and dyslipidemia
  • Smoking risk falls after quitting but does not return fully to baseline
  • First test: ankle-brachial index (≤0.9 abnormal)
exam_pearl: If the stem says he is a current smoker, smoking becomes the key; a remote quit date is what pushes this recall toward HTN/obesity.

stem: An 18-month-old child with normal growth and weight is brought by his parents. They are concerned because his older sibling has celiac disease. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: This recall's key is reassurance because the 18-month-old is asymptomatic with normal growth (50th percentile); a sibling's diagnosis raises risk but does not make this child ill. Screening of well first-degree relatives is usually deferred until about 2 to 3 years of age, after adequate gluten exposure, so nothing is needed today beyond reassurance and a plan to test later or sooner if symptoms appear. A gluten free diet must never be started without a confirmed diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. tTG-IgA (with total IgA) is the right first test when there are celiac symptoms (diarrhea, distension, failure to thrive), or as screening of an at-risk relative once older (about 2 to 3 years); this toddler is well and young, so testing can wait.
C. Starting a gluten free diet without serology and biopsy is wrong: it is unnecessary in a healthy child and causes false negative results if testing is later needed.
key_concept:
Celiac disease workup:
  • Symptoms or failure to thrive: tTG-IgA (with total IgA) while on gluten
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (do not stop gluten before)
  • Treatment: gluten free diet only after diagnosis
  • At-risk groups: first-degree relatives, type 1 diabetes, Down, Turner syndromes
exam_pearl: Never start a gluten free diet before testing; it masks the diagnosis.

stem: An 4-Year-Old child with normal growth and weight is brought by his parents. They are concerned because his older sibling has celiac disease. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: First-degree relatives of a patient with celiac disease are at high risk and should be screened even when asymptomatic. This child with "normal growth and weight" whose "older sibling has celiac disease" should have tTG IgA, the initial screening serology, while still eating gluten.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance misses a high-risk child; normal growth does not exclude celiac disease, which can be silent in relatives.
C. Starting a gluten-free diet before testing is wrong: gluten withdrawal makes serology and biopsy falsely negative, and diet is only started after the diagnosis is confirmed.
key_concept:
Celiac disease: serology, then biopsy, then diet.
  • Screen first-degree relatives and type 1 diabetes even without symptoms
  • Initial test: tTG IgA (with total IgA)
  • Confirm: endoscopy with duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia)
  • Test while on gluten
  • Treatment: lifelong gluten-free diet; tTG also monitors compliance
exam_pearl: Never start a gluten-free diet before serology and biopsy; it produces false-negative results.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2112).

stem: Pt after splenectomy surgery presented with multiple episodes of intestinal obstruction. Now complaining of abdominal distension, pain, rigidity, sluggish bowel sounds. Vitals stable. X ray air fluid level. What is the initial management?
why_right: Previous abdominal surgery (splenectomy) with "multiple episodes" of obstruction and air fluid levels on X ray means recurrent adhesive small bowel obstruction. An uncomplicated, soft abdomen would get NGT, fluids and bowel rest, but here the abdomen is "rigid", which signals peritonitis (possible strangulation or perforation). The recall's key is exploratory laparotomy because peritonitis is an absolute indication for surgery, so stable vitals do not change the decision.
why_wrong_block:
A. Paracentesis is for ascites (diagnostic or therapeutic), not for mechanical bowel obstruction with peritonism.
B. Gastrografin is a water soluble contrast study used in uncomplicated adhesive SBO to predict and help resolution; it is contraindicated once there are signs of peritonitis or strangulation.
D. NGT, analgesia and bowel rest is the correct first approach for uncomplicated SBO (soft abdomen, no peritonism); rigidity and recurrent episodes take this patient beyond conservative care.
key_concept:
Bowel obstruction: conservative first unless there is a surgical indication.
  • Uncomplicated: fluids, electrolytes, NG decompression, nil by mouth
  • Imaging: X ray first, CT confirms
  • Laparotomy if peritonitis (rigidity, rebound)
  • Laparotomy if strangulation (fever, tachycardia, constant pain, mesenteric stranding on CT)
  • Laparotomy if conservative management fails
  • Surgery years ago: adhesions; days ago: paralytic ileus
exam_pearl: The word "rigidity" turns a drip and suck SBO into an operative case even with normal vitals.

stem: Case for patient with PUD present with guarding and rigidity and rebound tenderness (perforation) What is the *initial* next step?
why_right: Guarding, rigidity and rebound in a PUD patient mean perforation with generalised peritonitis, which causes major third space fluid loss and early sepsis. The lead in asks for the "initial" step: resuscitate first (IV access, crystalloid fluids, with NPO, NG tube, PPI and antibiotics alongside), then take the patient to theatre once optimised.
why_wrong_block: B. Exploratory laparotomy with patch repair is the definitive treatment, but taking an under resuscitated, peritonitic patient straight to theatre is unsafe; it is the answer when the question asks for definitive or most appropriate management.
key_concept:
Perforated peptic ulcer sequence:
  • 1. ABC and IV fluid resuscitation (initial)
  • 2. NPO, NG tube, IV PPI, broad spectrum antibiotics, analgesia
  • 3. Erect chest X ray: free air under diaphragm; CT if unclear
  • 4. Laparotomy: duodenal ulcer, omental (Graham) patch; antral gastric ulcer, partial gastrectomy
  • 5. H. pylori eradication after repair
exam_pearl: "Initial" step = fluids; "definitive" or "most appropriate management" = laparotomy and patch repair.

stem: A case of hemolytic uremic syndrome diarrhea. Lab investigations was ordered. What are findings?
why_right: Diarrhea-associated HUS (Shiga toxin E. coli O157:H7) causes a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia: red cells are sheared in small vessels, producing fragmented RBCs (schistocytes) on the smear. Together with thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury this forms the HUS triad.
why_wrong_block:
A. Atypical lymphocytes are the smear finding of infectious mononucleosis (EBV), not HUS.
B. Eosinophilia suggests parasitic infection, allergy or drug reaction; it is not a feature of HUS.
key_concept:
HUS triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury.
  • Classic: child under 5 after bloody diarrhea (E. coli O157:H7, Shiga toxin)
  • Smear: schistocytes (helmet cells)
  • Schistocytes also in TTP, DIC, HELLP, mechanical valves
  • Treatment: supportive; avoid antibiotics
  • Most common cause of acute renal failure in children
exam_pearl: Fever and neurological signs in an adult with the same smear point to TTP (low ADAMTS13), not HUS.

stem: Pediatric with KNEE AND ANKLE (2 Joints) pain, limited range of motion, warmth, had gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago US shows effusion. How to MANAGE (It was management)
OptC: synovial aspiration for analysis and culture
why_right: Pain and swelling in two lower limb joints ("KNEE AND ANKLE") "2 weeks" after gastroenteritis is post-enteric reactive arthritis: a sterile, oligoarticular inflammatory arthritis. The effusion is sterile inflammation, and first-line treatment is an NSAID such as oral ibuprofen.
why_wrong_block:
B. Aspirin is avoided in children because of Reye syndrome risk; it is reserved for specific indications such as Kawasaki disease.
C. Synovial aspiration is the step for a single hot joint with fever or systemic toxicity where septic arthritis must be excluded; here two joints (oligoarticular) 2 weeks after an enteric infection, without fever, fits reactive arthritis.
D. IV antibiotics treat septic arthritis (usually one joint, febrile, toxic child), after aspiration and cultures; reactive arthritis is sterile.
key_concept:
Joint pain after infection in a child: count the joints and check for fever.
  • 2 or more joints, 1 to 4 weeks after gastroenteritis or urethritis: reactive arthritis, NSAID
  • Single hot joint, fever, refusal to move: septic arthritis, aspirate then IV antibiotics
  • Hip pain after viral URTI, well child: transient synovitis
  • Migratory arthritis after sore throat: acute rheumatic fever
exam_pearl: One joint plus fever flips the answer to synovial aspiration for analysis and culture.

stem: Pediatric with knee pain, limited range of motion, warmth, had gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago Xray shows No effusion How to MANAGE (It was management)
OptC: synovial aspiration for analysis and culture
why_right: This recall's key is synovial aspiration because a single warm knee with "limited range of motion" in a child is septic arthritis until proven otherwise, and joint fluid analysis with culture is the test that confirms or excludes it. Plain X-ray is insensitive for effusion, so "no effusion" on X-ray does not rule out a septic joint.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral ibuprofen treats reactive arthritis or transient synovitis, but only after septic arthritis is excluded in a monoarticular hot joint.
B. Aspirin is avoided in children (Reye syndrome) and does not address the need to exclude infection.
D. IV antibiotics are started for suspected septic arthritis, ideally after aspiration and cultures are taken; the diagnostic step comes first here.
key_concept:
Monoarticular hot joint in a child: exclude septic arthritis first.
  • Features: fever, warm tender joint, reduced ROM, refusal to bear weight
  • Ultrasound detects effusion better than X-ray
  • Key test: arthrocentesis with cell count, Gram stain and culture, plus blood culture
  • Most common organism: Staphylococcus aureus
  • Then empirical IV antibiotics
exam_pearl: Compare the paired card: two joints after gastroenteritis is reactive arthritis treated with ibuprofen; a single hot joint is aspirated.

stem: A 6 months old child known case cerebral palsy With recurrent episodes of pneumonia (Did They Say Aspiration?) And Failure To Thrive Despite Thickened Formula. Diagnosis of GERD is suspected. What is the most appropriate diagnostic approach?
highlight_terms_source: Failure To Thrive Despite Thickened Formula
why_right: This recall's key is a contrast upper GI study because this neurologically impaired infant has complicated reflux ("recurrent episodes of pneumonia", "failure to thrive despite thickened formula") and is heading towards surgical anti-reflux management. The contrast study shows anatomy (malrotation, hiatal hernia, stricture, obstruction) that can mimic or worsen GERD and is required before fundoplication.
why_wrong_block:
B. pH (or pH impedance) monitoring quantifies reflux and links it to symptoms such as cough or apnea; it confirms GERD but does not show the anatomy needed before surgery.
C. Endoscopy with biopsy assesses esophagitis, strictures or eosinophilic esophagitis; it is invasive and not the first study here.
D. A PPI trial is for uncomplicated symptoms in older children; in infants it is not a diagnostic test, and with aspiration pneumonias and failure to thrive objective evaluation is needed.
key_concept:
Infant GERD: physiological reflux vs complicated GERD.
  • Happy spitter, gaining weight: reassurance, feeding advice
  • Red flags: failure to thrive, recurrent pneumonia, apnea, Sandifer posturing
  • Contrast upper GI study: anatomy (malrotation, hiatal hernia, stricture), pre-surgery
  • pH impedance: quantify reflux, correlate with symptoms
  • Endoscopy: esophagitis or other mucosal disease
  • Cerebral palsy with refractory GERD: fundoplication with or without gastrostomy
exam_pearl: If the question asks for the most accurate test to confirm reflux itself, the answer is pH impedance monitoring, not the contrast study.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recaller note: this is the full recall in this exact order.

stem: Female patient aged 45 medically free no HTN or DM. BMI 38. She has a positive family history of premature cardiac death. LDL ~3.47 (higher than normal range) Whats the best counseling for her/lower her cardiovascular risk?
highlight_terms_source: positive family history of premature cardiac death
why_right: She is a 45-year-old woman with no hypertension and no diabetes and an LDL of about 3.47 mmol/L, far below the 4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL) threshold that mandates high-intensity statin. She has no clinical ASCVD, so this is primary prevention where her 10-year risk is likely low. Her main modifiable problem is BMI 38, so lifestyle modification (diet, exercise, weight loss) is the best counseling; the family history is a risk enhancer that matters if her calculated risk is borderline or intermediate.
why_wrong_block: A. High-intensity statin is for clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL), or high-risk diabetics; a normotensive non-diabetic with LDL 3.47 does not meet these.
key_concept:
Statin benefit groups (age >21):
  • Clinical ASCVD: high-intensity statin
  • LDL ≥190 mg/dL (≈4.9 mmol/L): high-intensity statin
  • Diabetes, 40 to 75 y, LDL 70 to 189: moderate (high if multiple risk factors or 10-y risk ≥20%)
  • No diabetes, 40 to 75 y, LDL 70 to 189, 10-y risk ≥7.5%: moderate to high
  • Everyone else: lifestyle first; family history is a risk enhancer, not an automatic statin trigger
exam_pearl: Mildly raised LDL plus obesity and no HTN/DM = lifestyle first; the LDL must reach ≈4.9 mmol/L before statin is automatic.

stem: Male Patient, 45 Years Old, Hypertensive And Smoker For 20 Years. Lipid Profile Shows: LDL 4.3, Total Cholesterol 6.1, Triglycerides Normal. What Is The Best Preventive Counseling?
OptB: Lifestyle Modifications And Recheck Lipid After 3 Months
OptC: Give Aspirin No Moderate Intensity Statin
why_right: This 45-year-old man has stacked risk factors: hypertension, 20 years of smoking, LDL 4.3 and total cholesterol 6.1 mmol/L. That combination puts his 10-year ASCVD risk in the range where statin therapy is recommended, so this recall's key is to start a statin now rather than wait. Lifestyle change and smoking cessation are added on top, not used as a substitute.
why_wrong_block:
B. Lifestyle alone with a 3-month recheck suits a low-risk person with mildly raised LDL (like a young normotensive non-smoker); with HTN plus heavy smoking, delaying statin is not appropriate.
C. Aspirin is not routine for primary prevention because bleeding risk offsets the benefit, and withholding a statin removes the key preventive drug.
key_concept:
Primary prevention statin decision = LDL level + 10-year ASCVD risk.
  • LDL ≥190 mg/dL (≈4.9 mmol/L) or clinical ASCVD: high-intensity statin
  • Age 40 to 75, LDL 70 to 189, risk ≥7.5%: moderate to high intensity
  • Several risk factors (HTN, smoking) push the risk up
  • Always add lifestyle and smoking cessation
  • Aspirin: not routine in primary prevention
exam_pearl: Same LDL range as a low-risk patient, but HTN plus long smoking history flips the answer from lifestyle to statin.

stem: A previously healthy 4-month-old uncircumcised boy is brought to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of fever. He has not had vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or nasal congestion. There has been no known contact with ill persons. He has continued to breastfeed and has not had a decrease in the number wet diapers. He is mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive. Examination shows no focus of infection. Urinary catheterization is performed (see lab results). Temperature 39.1 °C. Test Result Normal Values: pH 7.5 (4.3-8); Specific gravity 1010 (1001-1030); Protein Absent (Absent); Glucose Absent (Absent); Ketones Absent (Absent); Nitrite Positive (Absent); Leukocytes 30-40 (0-3 per high power field); Erythrocytes 5-10 (0-2 per high power field). Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical therapy?
highlight_terms_source: mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive
why_right: Positive nitrite with 30 to 40 leukocytes on a catheter sample in a febrile "uncircumcised" infant means febrile UTI. He is beyond the young infant age, "mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive", still breastfeeding with normal wet diapers, so he tolerates oral intake and can be treated with an oral agent such as cephalexin, which is as effective as IV therapy in this setting.
why_wrong_block:
B. Azithromycin (a macrolide) does not cover E. coli and other Gram negative uropathogens and has no role in UTI.
C. Cefepime is a broad spectrum antipseudomonal agent for hospital-acquired or resistant infections; a mild community UTI does not need it.
D. IV ceftriaxone is for infants under about 2 months, toxic appearance, vomiting or inability to take oral medication; none applies here.
key_concept:
Febrile UTI in infants: oral vs IV.
  • Diagnosis: catheter or suprapubic sample; nitrite and leukocytes support, culture confirms
  • Oral (cephalexin, cefixime, amoxicillin-clavulanate): well appearing, tolerating orals
  • IV (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime): young infants, toxic, vomiting, cannot take orals
  • Risk factors: uncircumcised male, fever ≥39 °C, VUR, constipation
exam_pearl: Add vomiting, toxic appearance or age under 2 months and the answer flips to IV ceftriaxone.

stem: A previously healthy 4-month-old uncircumcised boy is brought to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of fever. He has not had vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or nasal congestion. There has been no known contact with ill persons. He has continued to breastfeed and has not had a decrease in the number wet diapers. He is mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive. Examination shows no focus of infection. Urinary catheterization is performed (see lab results). Temperature 39.1 °C. Test Result Normal Values: pH 7.5 (4.3-8); Specific gravity 1010 (1001-1030); Protein Absent (Absent); Glucose Absent (Absent); Ketones Absent (Absent); Nitrite Positive (Absent); Leukocytes 30-40 (0-3 per high power field); Erythrocytes 5-10 (0-2 per high power field). Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical therapy?
highlight_terms_source: mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive
why_right: The decisive point is the route: a 4-month-old who is "mildly ill appearing but alert and interactive", still breastfeeding and with normal wet diapers can take oral medication, so an oral antibiotic is appropriate. The catheter sample (nitrite positive, leukocytes 30-40/HPF) supports a febrile UTI in an uncircumcised boy, and oral therapy works as well as IV in a non-toxic infant older than about 2 months. This recall's key is the oral option, recorded here as amoxicillin.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oral azithromycin: a macrolide with poor activity against E. coli and other Gram-negative uropathogens; it is used for atypical respiratory infections, not UTI.
C. IV cefepime: a broad-spectrum antipseudomonal agent kept for complicated, hospital-acquired or resistant infections; far too broad and needlessly IV for a mild community UTI.
D. IV ceftriaxone: right if the infant were under about 2 months, toxic looking, vomiting or unable to take oral fluids; this baby is alert and feeding.
key_concept:
Febrile UTI in infants: the route depends on age and how ill the child looks.
  • Over ~2 months, non-toxic, tolerating oral intake: oral antibiotic (cephalexin, cefixime, amoxicillin-clavulanate, per local susceptibility)
  • Under ~2 months, toxic, vomiting or unable to drink: IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime
  • UA support: pyuria, positive nitrite, positive leukocyte esterase
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by urine culture from catheter or suprapubic aspiration
  • Uncircumcised male infants are at higher risk
exam_pearl: "Alert, feeding, normal wet diapers" means oral; "toxic, vomiting or under 2 months" means IV ceftriaxone.

stem: Child with constipation and symptoms of cystitis/UTI. Most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
why_right: The child has "symptoms of cystitis/UTI", which need an antibiotic active against E. coli, and amoxicillin is the oral option offered. Constipation is a recognized risk factor for UTI because it impairs bladder emptying; it explains why the infection happened but does not change the need to treat it. Constipation should also be managed to prevent recurrence. Option C was not recorded.
why_wrong_block:
B. Metronidazole: covers anaerobes and protozoa (C. difficile, Giardia, bacterial vaginosis), not the Gram-negative organisms that cause UTI; constipation is not an infection to treat.
D. No treatment: right only for asymptomatic bacteriuria in a healthy child; a symptomatic UTI must be treated to relieve symptoms and prevent pyelonephritis and renal scarring.
key_concept:
Constipation + UTI: treat the infection AND the bowel.
  • UTI risk factors: constipation, VUR, posterior urethral valves, uncircumcised male infant, incomplete bladder emptying
  • Symptomatic UTI: oral antibiotic (amoxicillin if susceptible, cefixime, TMP-SMX, nitrofurantoin)
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria in a healthy child: no antibiotics
  • Treat constipation to reduce recurrences
exam_pearl: Constipation is a risk factor, not an indication for metronidazole; the UTI still needs a urinary antibiotic.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option C not recorded.

stem: A patient presents with dull chest pain that is not related to activity. The pain is more prominent after spicy meals or emotional stress and increases with lying flat. [Hb Not Mentioned] How to establish the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: chest pain that is not related to activity
why_right: Non-exertional chest pain made worse by spicy meals and lying flat is typical of GERD. In this version no anemia or other alarm feature is given, so there is no reason for endoscopy first. Ambulatory 24-hour pH monitoring is the test that objectively confirms reflux as the cause of the symptoms.
why_wrong_block:
A. Barium swallow assesses structure and motility in dysphagia (strictures, rings, achalasia); it does not confirm acid reflux.
B. Endoscopy is for alarm features (anemia, dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding, older age) or refractory symptoms; none is given here (compare the Hb 110 version, where endoscopy is the answer).
C. Manometry diagnoses motility disorders (achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm with dysphagia) and is done before fundoplication, not to diagnose reflux.
key_concept:
Reflux-type chest pain: alarm features pick the test.
  • No alarm features: clinical diagnosis/PPI trial; to objectively confirm GERD: 24 h pH (impedance) monitoring
  • Alarm features (anemia, dysphagia, weight loss, GI bleeding): endoscopy first
  • Refractory GERD, normal endoscopy: pH monitoring
  • Refractory GERD with esophagitis: manometry, then fundoplication
  • Dysphagia to liquids and solids: barium swallow, then manometry
exam_pearl: Twin recall: same stem with Hb 110 (anemia = alarm feature) changes the answer to endoscopy.

stem: A patient presents with dull chest pain that is not related to activity. The pain is more prominent after spicy meals or emotional stress and increases with lying flat. [Hb 110] How to establish the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: chest pain that is not related to activity
why_right: The pain pattern (worse with spicy meals and lying flat, unrelated to exertion) suggests reflux or peptic disease, but this version gives Hb 110, i.e. anemia. Anemia is an alarm feature suggesting mucosal blood loss (esophagitis, ulcer, malignancy), so upper endoscopy is needed to see the mucosa and biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Barium swallow is for dysphagia work-up or when endoscopy is contraindicated or unavailable; it cannot biopsy or reliably show a bleeding lesion.
C. Manometry is for motility disorders (achalasia, esophageal spasm) or before fundoplication, not for anemia with reflux symptoms.
D. pH monitoring confirms reflux when there are NO alarm features or when endoscopy is normal (the Hb-not-mentioned version); anemia needs direct visualization first.
key_concept:
Alarm features mean endoscopy first.
  • Anemia / iron deficiency
  • Dysphagia or odynophagia
  • Weight loss
  • GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena, isolated high urea)
  • Older age with new symptoms
  • Persistent vomiting
exam_pearl: Same stem without Hb = pH monitoring; add Hb 110 = endoscopy.

stem: A newborn presents with persistent bleeding after circumcision that does not stop with compression. There is a positive family history of a bleeding disorder affecting Mother's Brother (no labs). What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Two clues settle it: bleeding after circumcision in a newborn (a classic first sign of severe hemophilia) and a bleeding disorder in the mother's brother. An affected maternal uncle means an X-linked recessive pattern: the mother is a carrier and her son is affected. Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) is the most common X-linked bleeding disorder, so it is the most likely diagnosis. Expected labs: prolonged aPTT with normal PT and platelet count.
why_wrong_block:
B. Von Willebrand disease: usually autosomal dominant, affects both sexes and passes through either parent. It typically causes mild mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, gums, menorrhagia) and rarely severe neonatal circumcision bleeding; it fits best with mucosal bleeding and a parent of either sex affected.
C. DIC: secondary to a severe illness (sepsis, asphyxia, shock) in a sick neonate who bleeds from many sites; it is not inherited and would not explain a family history.
D. Platelet disorder: causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding, and most inherited platelet function disorders are autosomal; it fits best with petechiae or a low platelet count, not an X-linked history with circumcision bleeding.
key_concept:
Bleeding pattern + inheritance identifies the disorder.
  • Maternal uncle or male relatives on the mother's side affected: X-linked, so hemophilia A (VIII) or B (IX)
  • Hemophilia: prolonged aPTT, normal PT and platelets; deep bleeding (joints, muscles, circumcision)
  • VWD: autosomal, mucosal bleeding, normal or mildly prolonged aPTT, prolonged bleeding time
  • Platelet disorders: petechiae, mucosal bleeding
  • DIC: sick patient, prolonged PT and aPTT, low platelets and fibrinogen
exam_pearl: "Mother's brother" means X-linked, so hemophilia; mucosal bleeding with both sexes affected suggests VWD.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-0374 → B. Von Willebrand disease. Confirm before the exam.

stem: A 3 years old came with unilateral undescended testis and no scrotum in the affected side what other conditions could be accompanied (something like this in surgery and medical part not pedi) Which of the following is associated Finding?
why_right: An undescended testis with an underdeveloped hemiscrotum on the "affected side" is cryptorchidism. The testis descends with the processus vaginalis, and in most undescended testes this processus stays patent, so an indirect inguinal hernia is the most common associated finding (usually repaired at the same time as orchidopexy).
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypospadias is associated with cryptorchidism too, but it is the association asked when the question focuses on sexual development or DSD; as a general associated finding the patent processus (hernia) is commoner.
C. Pyloric stenosis is a first born male infant problem with projectile non bilious vomiting at around 6 weeks; it has no link to testicular descent.
D. Congenital heart disease is not a typical association of isolated cryptorchidism; it suggests a syndrome (e.g. Noonan, Down) only when other features are given.
key_concept:
Undescended testis essentials:
  • Most common association: indirect inguinal hernia (patent processus vaginalis)
  • Genital association: hypospadias (if both, consider DSD workup)
  • Palpable testis: orchidopexy
  • Non palpable testis: diagnostic laparoscopy
  • Long term risks: infertility and testicular cancer
exam_pearl: Generic "associated finding" = inguinal hernia; "related to sexual development" = hypospadias.

stem: A 3 years old came with unilateral undescended testis and no scrotum in the affected side what other conditions could be accompanied (something like this in surgery and medical part not pedi) Which of the following is associated with this finding and related to sexual development?
why_right: The lead in narrows the question to an association "related to sexual development". Cryptorchidism and hypospadias are both disorders of male genital development that share androgen related causes, so they often coexist; hypospadias with an undescended testis should prompt evaluation for a disorder of sex development.
why_wrong_block:
B. Inguinal hernia is the most common associated finding overall (patent processus vaginalis), but it is a structural defect, not a disorder of sexual development.
C. Pyloric stenosis causes projectile non bilious vomiting in a young infant and is unrelated to genital development.
D. Congenital heart disease is not linked to sexual development and is only expected when a syndrome is described.
key_concept:
Cryptorchidism associations by lead in:
  • General associated finding: inguinal hernia
  • Related to sexual development: hypospadias
  • Hypospadias + undescended (especially non palpable) testis: evaluate for DSD (karyotype)
  • Cryptorchidism: most common disorder of sexual differentiation in boys
exam_pearl: Same stem, different lead in: "sexual development" flips the answer from hernia to hypospadias.

stem: A male has readings of high blood pressure. he doesn't exercise, high salt intake, and has stressful job. bp 138/88 (or 98 not sure) Na 160 other labs normal what is the INITIAL approach to manage this patient?
OptB: lower salt intake and enhance physical activity
OptC: advice to monitor bp and record the readings (something like that)
why_right: He has repeated raised readings around 138/88 with clear lifestyle drivers (no exercise, high salt intake, stress) and no target organ damage. At this level the INITIAL management is lifestyle modification: reduce salt, increase physical activity, manage weight and stress. Drugs are added only if BP stays above target despite lifestyle change or if overall cardiovascular risk is high.
why_wrong_block:
A. Immediate drug therapy is for BP ≥160/100, target organ damage, or high cardiovascular risk; 138/88 without these starts with lifestyle change.
C. Home or ambulatory monitoring is right to CONFIRM a single raised office reading (especially near 140/90); here readings are already raised and lifestyle advice is indicated regardless.
key_concept:
Raised BP: confirm, then lifestyle first, drugs by level and risk.
  • Single office reading: confirm with home/ambulatory BP
  • High-normal / stage 1 without target organ damage: lifestyle first
  • Stage 1 not responding: add a first-line drug (ACEi/ARB, CCB, thiazide)
  • ≥160/100 or target organ damage: start drugs now (with lifestyle)
  • Lifestyle: salt restriction, exercise, weight loss, limit alcohol
exam_pearl: The serum Na of 160 is almost certainly a recall artifact; dietary salt does not cause marked hypernatremia, so do not let it drive the answer.

stem: Old male came to the travel clinic. He has a 14 hour flight and his friend told him about DVT And he came for advice on how to prevent it?
key_concept:
Long-haul flight VTE prevention is graded by risk.
  • All travelers: mobilize, calf exercises, aisle seat, hydration
  • Increased risk: add properly fitted below-knee compression stockings
  • Very high risk: consider prophylactic LMWH, individualized
  • Aspirin is not recommended for travel VTE prevention
exam_pearl: Age alone does not justify an anticoagulant for a flight; the answer climbs the ladder only with added risk factors.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No option marked.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 70 years old Came to er after 12h complain of symptoms with rt side weakness. Ct showed: posterior artery occlusion with mild to moderate ischemic core Management?
why_right: He presents at 12 hours, beyond the 4.5-hour IV thrombolysis window, with a large-vessel occlusion and only a mild-to-moderate ischemic core, meaning salvageable brain remains. Mechanical thrombectomy is indicated for selected large-vessel occlusions up to 24 hours from last known well, for anterior circulation and, from recent trials, basilar (posterior) occlusion too. The other version of this recall describes a proximal anterior circulation occlusion; the management is the same.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV tPA is limited to 4.5 hours from onset (or last known well); at 12 hours it adds bleeding risk without proven benefit.
B. Observation (supportive care, antiplatelet) fits when there is no vessel to open or the tissue is already fully infarcted with no salvageable brain; here an occluded large vessel with a mild-to-moderate core still has tissue to save.
D. Bridging tPA plus thrombectomy is used when the patient arrives within 4.5 hours; at 12 hours only thrombectomy is given.
key_concept:
Acute ischemic stroke: time and vessel decide.
  • Step 1: glucose, then noncontrast CT to exclude bleed
  • ≤4.5 h, no contraindication: IV thrombolysis
  • LVO within 4.5 h: tPA plus thrombectomy
  • LVO 6 to 24 h with small/moderate core on imaging: thrombectomy alone
  • Large core within 24 h: thrombectomy now considered in selected patients (recent trials)
  • No LVO and outside 4.5 h: supportive care, aspirin within 24 to 48 h
exam_pearl: Past 4.5 hours, tPA drops out, but thrombectomy stays on the table up to 24 hours if the core is not large.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q): right sided weakness that started 12 hours ago, proximal anterior circulation occlusion, moderate size infarct core; options A- tPA, B- Mechanical thrombectomy (highlighted), C- Observation, D- tPA and mechanical thrombectomy.

stem: 68 years old came to the er with 3 days history of bilateral leg weakness and brisk movements reflexes in both legs, with urine retention and inability to walk and sensory level of T10. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: Bilateral leg weakness with brisk reflexes (upper motor neuron), urinary retention and a sensory level at T10 localizes to the thoracic spinal cord. In a 68-year-old with a 3-day course, the most likely cause is spinal cord compression (often metastatic epidural disease or degenerative/disc), which needs urgent whole-spine MRI and steroids.
why_wrong_block:
A. Transverse myelitis also gives a sensory level, UMN signs and bladder involvement, but it typically affects younger patients, often after infection or with MS/NMO, and MRI shows no compressive lesion.
B. GBS is an ascending polyneuropathy with areflexia and no sensory level; brisk reflexes exclude it.
C. Cauda equina is a lower motor neuron root lesion below L1: reduced or absent reflexes, saddle anesthesia and back pain, not hyperreflexia with a T10 level.
key_concept:
Leg weakness plus bladder: localize first.
  • Sensory level + UMN signs + bladder: spinal cord (myelopathy)
  • Older patient, acute/subacute: compression (metastases, disc, abscess) until MRI proves otherwise
  • Younger, post-infectious, no compressive lesion: transverse myelitis
  • Areflexia, ascending, no sensory level: GBS
  • LMN signs, saddle anesthesia: cauda equina
  • Work-up: urgent whole-spine MRI; give dexamethasone if malignancy suspected
exam_pearl: Sensory level plus brisk reflexes means cord, not roots or nerves; age then tips compression over myelitis.

stem: A hairdresser came to the emergency department with a swollen finger after pulling the skin around the nail a few days ago. Nail bed is intact
highlight_terms_source: pulling the skin around the nail
why_right: Swelling of the finger a few days after "pulling the skin around the nail" (a hangnail) with an "intact" nail bed is acute paronychia: infection of the soft tissue fold around the nail, usually Staph aureus, after minor trauma to the cuticle. Occupations with repeated manipulation or wet work (hairdressers, cleaners) are typical.
why_wrong_block:
A. Felon is an abscess of the closed pulp space of the fingertip, with a tense, throbbing, very painful pad, usually after a puncture wound; here the problem is at the nail fold.
C. Onychomycosis is a chronic fungal infection of the nail plate (thickened, discoloured, brittle nail) without acute swelling; here the nail is intact and the onset is acute.
D. Cellulitis is diffuse spreading redness of skin and subcutis, often with fever; the localised periungual swelling after a hangnail is more specifically paronychia.
key_concept:
Finger infections by site:
  • Nail fold (periungual): paronychia, after hangnail or nail biting; abscess needs incision and drainage
  • Chronic paronychia: wet work, often Candida
  • Pulp of fingertip: felon, urgent drainage
  • Nail plate: onychomycosis
  • Flexor sheath: Kanavel signs, flexor tenosynovitis
  • Diffuse skin redness: cellulitis
exam_pearl: Nail fold = paronychia; fingertip pulp = felon.

stem: Patient Known case of UC, Presented with severe Bloody diarrhea, Patient is very sick. What to Add after IV fluid?
why_right: A known UC patient with "severe bloody diarrhea" who is "very sick" has acute severe ulcerative colitis (frequent bloody stools plus systemic toxicity). After resuscitation with IV fluids, the next step is IV corticosteroids, and IV methylprednisolone (or IV hydrocortisone) is the standard first line induction agent. IV route is chosen because a toxic patient needs reliable, rapid, high dose steroid effect.
why_wrong_block:
A. Azathioprine is a slow acting steroid sparing agent used for maintenance of remission; it takes weeks to work and has no role in rescuing an acute severe flare.
C. Oral prednisone is used for moderate flares in an outpatient who is not toxic; a very sick patient with severe bloody diarrhea needs IV steroids.
key_concept:
Acute severe UC: IV fluids then IV steroids, reassess at day 3.
  • Definition: 6 or more bloody stools/day PLUS systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, anemia, raised ESR/CRP)
  • First line: IV methylprednisolone or IV hydrocortisone
  • Also: VTE prophylaxis, stool tests to exclude C. difficile
  • No response at about day 3: rescue with infliximab or ciclosporin
  • Failure of rescue, toxic megacolon or perforation: colectomy
  • Azathioprine and 5-ASA: maintenance, not rescue
exam_pearl: Mild to moderate flare = oral steroid or 5-ASA; "very sick" or toxic = admit and give IV steroid.

stem: A patient with pneumonia is agitated, pH 7.1, and PaO₂ 7 kPa. What is the best management?
why_right: This patient has severe respiratory failure from pneumonia: profound hypoxemia ("PaO2 7 kPa"), severe acidemia ("pH 7.1") and he is "agitated". Altered mental status and agitation mean he cannot protect his airway or tolerate a mask, and the degree of acidosis predicts failure of non-invasive support, so controlled (elective) intubation and mechanical ventilation is the safest step.
why_wrong_block: B. BiPAP needs an alert, cooperative patient who can protect the airway; it is best for hypercapnic COPD exacerbations with moderate acidosis. An agitated patient with pH 7.1 and severe hypoxemic pneumonia is a contraindication and delaying intubation worsens outcome.
key_concept:
NIV vs intubation: decide on mental status, airway protection and severity.
  • NIV (BiPAP): alert, cooperative, hypercapnic (classically COPD), moderate acidosis
  • Intubate: agitated, confused or drowsy, cannot protect airway, copious secretions
  • Intubate: severe acidosis, refractory hypoxemia, hemodynamic instability
  • Intubate: NIV trial failing or worsening ABG
exam_pearl: Any altered consciousness (agitated, drowsy, confused) with respiratory failure pushes the answer from NIV to intubation.

stem: A patient presents with a firm, painless, raised pink papule. Upon taking history the patient told you she had an old scar due to burn. What is the type of ulcer?
why_right: A new lesion arising in an "old scar due to burn" is Marjolin ulcer: malignant change, most often squamous cell carcinoma, in a chronic scar or non healing wound, typically many years after the injury. A firm, raised, painless lesion in a burn scar must be biopsied to confirm it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Arterial ulcers are painful, punched out ulcers on the toes or pressure points with absent pulses and ischaemic skin; they are not linked to burn scars.
B. Cushing ulcer is a stress peptic ulcer of the stomach or duodenum after head injury or raised intracranial pressure; it is not a skin lesion.
D. Neuropathic ulcers occur on pressure points of an insensate foot (diabetes, leprosy) and are painless but punched out with callus; they do not arise in burn scars.
key_concept:
Ulcer eponyms and types:
  • Marjolin: SCC in a chronic burn scar or non healing wound; treat with biopsy, then wide excision
  • Curling: stress gastric or duodenal ulcer after major burns
  • Cushing: stress ulcer after head injury or raised ICP
  • Arterial: painful, absent pulses
  • Venous: gaiter area, intact pulses, dark skin
  • Neuropathic: painless, pressure points, insensate foot
exam_pearl: Burns + skin lesion in the scar = Marjolin; burns + GI bleed = Curling ulcer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): 60-year-old woman with an erythematous, oozing, painful lesion on her left arm with history of burn injury on the same side; options Neuropathic / Ulcer / Marjolin; Marjolin highlighted.

stem: Pediatric patient was brought to ED with decreased level of consciousness. BP 75/55 HR 300/min ECG picture: SVT Whats the appropriate immediate management?
why_right: The child is unstable: "decreased level of consciousness" and BP 75/55 with SVT at 300/min. In any tachyarrhythmia the first question is stability, and unstable SVT is treated with immediate synchronized electrical cardioversion. Drugs and vagal maneuvers are steps for the stable patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amiodarone: a second-line antiarrhythmic for refractory SVT in a stable child, usually with expert advice; it is slow to act and can worsen hypotension.
B. Vagal maneuvers: the first step in a stable child with SVT (ice to the face in infants, Valsalva in older children); they waste time in a child with altered consciousness and hypotension.
C. Adenosine: the drug of choice for stable SVT after vagal maneuvers fail; in an unstable child it may be tried only if IV access is already in place and it causes no delay, but cardioversion is the standard answer when consciousness is impaired.
key_concept:
SVT ladder: check stability first.
  • Unstable (hypotension, altered consciousness, shock, heart failure): synchronized cardioversion
  • Stable: vagal maneuvers first
  • Then adenosine (rapid push, escalating dose)
  • Then other agents (CCB in older patients, amiodarone or procainamide in children) or cardioversion
  • Avoid verapamil in infants
exam_pearl: Same ECG, different answer: an alert child with normal BP gets vagal maneuvers or adenosine; drowsy and hypotensive gets synchronized cardioversion.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version: An 8-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department. He is alert, with BP 75/50 mmHg and HR 130/min. His ECG is shown (narrow complex tachycardia). Options Adenosine / Amiodarone / Vagal stimulation / Synchronized electrical cardioversion; D highlighted. Answer D: Unstable px with SVT.

stem: A child with a painless neck nodule that moves up and down, moves up with tongue protrusion. What is the most appropriate treatment ?
why_right: A painless midline neck nodule in a child that "moves up with tongue protrusion" is a thyroglossal duct cyst, a remnant of the thyroid's descent tract that is attached to the hyoid. Treatment is surgical excision by the Sistrunk procedure (cyst, tract and central part of the hyoid), which prevents recurrence and recurrent infection; ultrasound is done first to confirm a normal thyroid elsewhere.
why_wrong_block:
B. Needle aspiration only empties the cyst temporarily; the epithelial tract remains, so it recurs and can become infected. Aspiration is not definitive treatment.
C. Reassurance is wrong because thyroglossal cysts do not regress, tend to get infected, and rarely harbour carcinoma; they should be excised.
key_concept:
Pediatric neck masses:
  • Midline, moves with tongue protrusion: thyroglossal cyst; Sistrunk excision
  • Lateral, anterior to sternocleidomastoid: branchial cleft cyst; excision
  • Lateral, soft, transilluminates: cystic hygroma; sclerotherapy, then surgery
  • Moves with swallowing only: thyroid origin
  • Before excision: US to confirm a normal thyroid gland
exam_pearl: Excision must include the middle of the hyoid (Sistrunk); simple cyst excision recurs.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original recall: Pedia Pt with typical symptoms of thyroglossal cyst (not written). What is the management? A. Surgical excision. The fuller 'Possible Recall' is used as stem.

stem: A 60-year-old man complaining of right knee pain for several years that has increased over the last few months. He also has noticed frequent knee clicks. A diagnosis of osteoarthritis is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
why_right: A 60-year-old with years of knee pain, slowly worsening, with clicks (crepitus) has the classic picture of osteoarthritis. OA is a clinical diagnosis: in patients aged 45 or over with activity-related pain and little or no morning stiffness, no test is needed to confirm it. The lead-in asks how to confirm the diagnosis, not what baseline imaging to order.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bilateral knee X-rays: not needed to confirm OA, and X-ray changes correlate poorly with symptoms. Right when the stem asks for baseline imaging or there are atypical features (choose standing films).
B. MRI of the right knee: reserved for suspected internal derangement (meniscal or ligament injury with locking or giving way) or an unclear diagnosis.
D. Arthroscopy for the right knee: invasive and has no role in diagnosing OA; used only for selected mechanical problems.
key_concept:
OA is diagnosed clinically; imaging is for atypical cases or baseline.
  • Age ≥ 45 + activity-related pain + short (≤ 30 min) morning stiffness = clinical OA
  • 'Confirm the diagnosis' = no further investigation
  • 'Baseline/next imaging' = standing (weight-bearing) plain X-ray
  • X-ray: joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts
exam_pearl: Read the verb: 'confirm suspected OA' means no test; 'next investigation' in OA means standing X-ray.

stem: Child with a known fatty acid oxidation defect (detoxification) develops fatigue and hypoglycemia following a viral illness. Which of the following measures is most effective in preventing metabolic decompensation during future illness episodes?
why_right: Fatty acid oxidation defects prevent the body from using fat for energy and ketones during fasting or catabolic stress, so illness causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia and metabolic crisis. The key to prevention is to avoid fasting and supply carbohydrate during illness: a sick-day plan of frequent glucose-containing feeds, with early IV dextrose (continuous glucose infusion) if the child cannot take orals. A steady glucose supply suppresses lipolysis and prevents decompensation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Fasting to promote ketone production: the opposite of correct; these children cannot oxidize fat to make ketones, so fasting is the trigger for hypoglycemia and crisis.
C. High-fat diet: increases the load on the defective pathway; long-chain defects are managed with a low long-chain fat diet, often supplemented with MCT.
D. Protein restriction: the mainstay for urea cycle disorders and organic acidemias (hyperammonemia), not for fatty acid oxidation defects.
key_concept:
Fatty acid oxidation defect (e.g. MCAD): never let them fast.
  • Crisis: hypoketotic hypoglycemia after fasting or viral illness, lethargy, possible hepatomegaly and cardiomyopathy
  • Prevention: frequent feeds, avoid prolonged fasting, sick-day carbohydrate plan
  • Unable to take orals: early IV dextrose infusion
  • Long-chain defects: restrict long-chain fat, use MCT
  • Urea cycle defects / organic acidemias: protein restriction
exam_pearl: Hypoglycemia WITHOUT ketones after fasting or illness suggests a fatty acid oxidation defect: give glucose, never fast.

stem: A school-aged child with asthma came to the ER with acute asthma exacerbation, SpO2 95%, peak flow meter at best 60, can complete full sentences, took two puffs of salbutamol at home, mild wheeze on auscultation. Which is the most appropriate management?
OptD: Give salbutamol by spacer then reassess
why_right: This is a mild to moderate exacerbation: SpO2 95% (above 92%), "can complete full sentences" and only "mild wheeze", and a peak flow of about 60% of best is above the 50% cut-off for a severe attack. The first step is an inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist given by spacer (as effective as a nebulizer in mild/moderate attacks), followed by reassessment of symptoms and peak flow to decide what comes next.
why_wrong_block:
A. Start oral corticosteroids and hospitalize: hospitalization is for severe or life-threatening attacks (SpO2 below 92%, too breathless to talk, poor response to bronchodilators). Systemic steroids are part of exacerbation care, but this child needs bronchodilator and reassessment first, not admission.
B. Add salmeterol and hospitalize: salmeterol is a long-acting controller with slow onset, not a reliever, and is never used alone in asthma; admission is not indicated for a mild attack.
C. Add ipratropium: added to repeated salbutamol in severe or life-threatening exacerbations or poor response to SABA, not as the first step in a mild attack.
key_concept:
Acute asthma in children: classify severity, then treat.
  • Mild/moderate: SpO2 above 92%, talks in full sentences, minimal accessory muscle use: SABA via spacer, reassess
  • Severe: SpO2 below 92%, too breathless to talk or feed, PEFR 33-50%: oxygen, repeated SABA + ipratropium, systemic steroids
  • Life-threatening: silent chest, cyanosis, altered consciousness, PEFR below 33%: add IV magnesium, ICU
  • Order: oxygen if needed, SABA, systemic steroids, reassess, escalate
exam_pearl: Full sentences and SpO2 above 92% mean spacer salbutamol and reassess; unable to talk or SpO2 below 92% means severe, so add ipratropium and steroids.

stem: 6-month-old infant presents with a history of recurrent cough and upper respiratory tract infections (URTI) about 7–8 episodes over the past year. What should we do?
OptC: Refer to ENT for tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy
why_right: About "7-8 episodes" of cough/URTI a year is within the normal range for an infant or young child, especially with siblings or daycare exposure. Without red flags (failure to thrive, severe or unusual infections, pneumonias, chronic wet cough) no investigation or intervention is needed. The useful step is reassurance plus hand hygiene, the single most effective measure to reduce spread of respiratory viruses.
why_wrong_block:
B. Prophylactic low-dose antibiotics: URTIs are viral, so antibiotics give no benefit and promote resistance; prophylaxis has a role in selected conditions (e.g. asplenia, rheumatic fever, some recurrent UTI) but not in normal childhood colds.
C. Tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy: considered for frequent, documented recurrent tonsillitis or obstructive sleep apnea from adenotonsillar hypertrophy, not for simple colds in a 6-month-old.
key_concept:
Recurrent URTIs in young children are usually normal.
  • Several viral URTIs per year is normal in infants and toddlers, more with daycare or siblings
  • Management: reassurance, hand hygiene, avoid smoke exposure
  • Red flags for immunodeficiency or CF: failure to thrive, recurrent pneumonia, severe or unusual bacterial infections, chronic wet cough, steatorrhea
  • Red flags call for workup (immunoglobulins, sweat chloride), not antibiotics
exam_pearl: Frequent colds in a thriving infant: reassure and advise hand hygiene; recurrent pneumonias or failure to thrive: investigate.

stem: 50 years old male patient K/C of DM . He did open abdominal surgery. In the 3rd post-operative days, he develop redness and swelling at the surgical site maybe tender swelling. Vitally stable (I think they mentioned no fever). What is the best management?
highlight_terms_source: redness and swelling at the surgical site
why_right: Redness and tender swelling at the incision on post-operative day 3 in a diabetic is read by this recall as a surgical site infection with infected or devitalized tissue in the wound. The source's reasoning is source control: open the wound, drain any pus and debride dead tissue, because antibiotics cannot penetrate a collection or necrotic tissue, and diabetes raises the risk of rapid deep spread. On that reading, surgical debridement is the best management.
why_wrong_block:
B. Empiric IV antibiotics are an adjunct (for surrounding cellulitis, systemic signs or immunocompromise), not a substitute for opening and debriding an infected wound with a collection.
C. A wound swab is taken when the wound is opened, but observing an established infection in a diabetic delays source control and risks deep or necrotizing spread.
D. Reassurance fits a seroma (painless swelling without redness or fever); here the wound is red and tender, which is infection.
key_concept:
Post-operative wound problems: identify the collection, then drain it.
  • Superficial SSI: open the wound, drain, debride, dress
  • Wound abscess: incision and drainage
  • Seroma: painless swelling, no redness or fever
  • Small intra-abdominal collection: antibiotics
  • Large collection: percutaneous drainage under imaging
  • Unstable patient: laparotomy
exam_pearl: Antibiotics treat cellulitis; pus or dead tissue in a wound needs a knife, not a drip.

stem: An 18-month-old child is brought by his mother to the well-baby clinic for MMR vaccination. He has an upper respiratory tract infection, fever of 38.9°C, and congested throat. On examination, the child appears slightly ill. Regarding vaccination what is the best option?
OptB: Postpone vaccination until the child recovers
OptC: Give the MMR vaccine without rubella component
OptD: The second dose should be given at 4 year
why_right: A mild acute illness such as an URTI, with or without fever, is not a contraindication to MMR or other vaccines. The child looks only "slightly ill", so he should be vaccinated on schedule; deferring creates missed opportunities and leaves him unprotected. Postponement is a precaution only for a moderate to severe illness, where an ill-looking child is the deciding factor, not the thermometer alone.
why_wrong_block:
B. Postpone vaccination until recovery: right only for a moderate or severe acute illness (child looks unwell or toxic); a mild URTI in a slightly ill child does not justify delay.
C. Give MMR without the rubella component: there is no valid reason to drop a component; the combined vaccine is given, and true contraindications (severe allergy, e.g. to neomycin or gelatin, pregnancy, significant immunosuppression) apply to the whole live vaccine.
D. The second dose should be given at 4 years: does not answer what to do today; in the Saudi schedule the 18-month visit is itself an MMR dose, with another at school entry.
key_concept:
Vaccination and intercurrent illness.
  • Mild illness with or without fever: vaccinate
  • Current antibiotics or recovering from illness: vaccinate
  • Moderate/severe acute illness: defer until better (precaution)
  • MMR true contraindications: severe allergy to a component (neomycin, gelatin), pregnancy, severe immunodeficiency
  • Saudi MMR doses: 12 months, 18 months, school entry
exam_pearl: "Slightly ill" means vaccinate; "looks ill" or toxic means postpone.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot version: child visiting to get vaccine with mild fever (maybe 37) and flu-like symptoms; options Give vaccine / postpone / give inactivated and leave live attenuated. Alhomrani note: the confirmed recall literally said '38.9 AND looks SLIGHTLY ill'. Temperature differs between recalls (37 to 38.9, but not 39); in all cases answer is the same (give vaccine), unless 39 or above, then double check. If a new recall says 'looks ill' without 'slightly', reconsider. As per Nelson & UTD: mild illness with or without fever is not a contraindication for MMR.

stem: 10y/o (I’m not sure about the age) with cystic fibrosis asking when to screen for T1DM ?
OptC: No need to screen until equal or more than 18
why_right: The diabetes screened for in cystic fibrosis is CF-related diabetes (the recall says T1DM), caused by progressive pancreatic damage. Guidelines recommend an annual oral glucose tolerance test starting by age 10, because CFRD often shows only postprandial hyperglycemia that fasting glucose misses. HbA1c is unreliable in CF.
why_wrong_block:
A. HbA1c every 6 months: HbA1c underestimates glycemia in CF (increased red cell turnover) and is not sensitive enough to screen; it is used to monitor once diabetes is diagnosed, not to screen.
B. Fasting blood glucose annually: early CFRD causes post-meal hyperglycemia with normal fasting glucose, so FBG misses many cases.
C. No need to screen until 18 or older: screening starts in childhood (by age 10) because CFRD is common in adolescents and worsens lung function and nutrition.
key_concept:
CF-related diabetes screening.
  • Test: annual 2-hour 75 g OGTT
  • Start: by age 10 in all CF patients
  • HbA1c: falsely low in CF, not for screening
  • Fasting glucose: often normal early
  • Treatment of CFRD: insulin
exam_pearl: CF patient + diabetes screening = annual OGTT from age 10; HbA1c is the classic wrong answer.

stem: 63-year-old man presents with multiple psychiatric symptoms, including prominent visual hallucinations. He started on donepezil, which improved his cognition but visual hallucinations persist. what to add?
why_right: Cognition improved on donepezil but prominent visual hallucinations persist. When hallucinations remain distressing despite a cholinesterase inhibitor, a low-dose atypical antipsychotic is added, and quetiapine is preferred because its weak dopamine D2 blockade makes it least likely to worsen parkinsonism or cause severe sensitivity reactions, particularly if this is dementia with Lewy bodies, where visual hallucinations are a core feature.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sertraline treats depression or anxiety, not psychotic symptoms; it is right if the dominant problem is low mood.
C. Amitriptyline is a tricyclic with strong anticholinergic effects that worsen confusion and can provoke hallucinations in dementia, and it opposes donepezil; it is used for neuropathic pain or depression in younger patients.
D. Donepezil has improved his cognition and cholinesterase inhibitors can reduce hallucinations in Lewy body disease, so stopping it removes benefit; it is stopped for intolerance.
key_concept:
Persistent hallucinations in dementia despite a cholinesterase inhibitor: add a low-dose atypical antipsychotic, quetiapine preferred.
  • DLB: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder
  • DLB patients are very sensitive to antipsychotics; avoid typicals such as haloperidol
  • Quetiapine or clozapine have the least D2 blockade
  • Avoid anticholinergic drugs (tricyclics) in dementia
exam_pearl: In dementia with hallucinations, haloperidol is the trap; quetiapine is the safer choice.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original typed recall: Alzheimer's scenario on donepezil, full improvement after 6 months but still visual hallucinations, how to adjust meds; options ADD quetiapine / ADD amitryptaline / Switch donepezil to rivastigmine; ADD quetiapine highlighted. Q: version states Answer: B.

stem: infant came with 4 times watery diarrhea, no fever, systemic unremarkable Your management?
why_right: An infant with "4 times watery diarrhea", "no fever" and an unremarkable systemic exam has simple acute (usually viral) gastroenteritis with no sign of significant dehydration. The cornerstone of management is oral rehydration solution with continued breast or formula feeding, plus reassurance and return precautions. Nothing here suggests the child cannot drink or is severely dry.
why_wrong_block:
B. IV normal saline with admission is for severe dehydration (lethargy, poor perfusion), persistent vomiting with inability to take oral fluids, or failure of ORS; this infant is well.
C. Stool culture is reserved for bloody or mucoid diarrhea, high fever or toxicity, outbreaks, or immunocompromise; it does not change management of simple watery diarrhea.
D. Drugs (antidiarrheals, antiemetics, antibiotics) are not used routinely in infant watery diarrhea; antibiotics need a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial cause, and antimotility agents are unsafe in young children.
key_concept:
Acute watery diarrhea in a well infant = ORS + continue feeding + reassurance.
  • No or mild to moderate dehydration and able to drink: ORS
  • Replace ongoing losses after each stool or vomit
  • IV fluids: severe dehydration, cannot tolerate oral intake, or ORS fails
  • No routine antibiotics, antidiarrheals or antiemetics
  • Do not change or dilute milk
exam_pearl: Admission and IV fluids only enter the answer when the stem gives severe dehydration signs or inability to drink.

stem: paediatric with watery diarrhea and vomiting what investigation to do
key_concept:
Watery + vomiting = think viral; bloody/mucoid + toxic = think bacterial.
  • Viral gastroenteritis: stool antigen (ELISA) or PCR; management supportive
  • Invasive bacterial diarrhea: stool culture
  • Fecal leukocytes point to inflammatory (bacterial) diarrhea, they do not confirm viral disease
  • Enteric viruses are found in stool, not by serum culture or serology

A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Stool antigen.
exam_pearl: The word "watery" with vomiting in a child steers to viral antigen testing; blood in the stool flips it to culture.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Recall text: 'what investigation to do stool antigen another was culture' (options incomplete, no answer marked).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: infant (3M) with signs of pneumonia and in examination there was bilateral crepitations, he was dehydrated and distressed, no vital signs given
why_right: A 3-month-old with "bilateral crepitations" who is "dehydrated and distressed" needs immediate supportive stabilization first: clear the airway (nasal suction), correct dehydration, and give low-flow oxygen. In an infant this age, diffuse bilateral crackles most often reflect a viral lower respiratory infection such as bronchiolitis, where management is supportive. The lead-in asks what to do now, and airway, breathing and hydration come before investigations.
why_wrong_block: A. IV antibiotics and chest X-ray do not address the immediate problems (secretions, distress, dehydration); chest X-ray is not routine in bronchiolitis, and antibiotics are added when bacterial pneumonia is suspected (high fever, toxic look, focal consolidation) after the child is stabilized.
key_concept:
Distressed, dehydrated infant with chest infection: stabilize first (ABC).
  • Suction nasal secretions (infants are obligate nasal breathers)
  • Oxygen for distress or low saturation
  • Hydration: IV or NG if unable to feed
  • Bronchiolitis: supportive only; no steroids, no routine antibiotics or CXR
  • Inability to maintain oral intake is itself an admission criterion
exam_pearl: A sick infant with diffuse crackles: supportive care beats antibiotics unless the stem gives clear bacterial clues.

stem: Patient presents after 30 minutes of slurred speech that resolved, no trauma or drug use or fever. Carotid shows stenosis 48% Best management besides controlling risk factors?
highlight_terms_source: 30 minutes of slurred speech that resolved
why_right: Thirty minutes of slurred speech that fully resolved is a TIA, and carotid imaging shows 48% stenosis, which is below the 50% level at which revascularization is considered for a symptomatic patient. Below that level there is no benefit from endarterectomy or stenting, so management is best medical therapy and observation: antiplatelet, statin and control of blood pressure, glucose and smoking.
why_wrong_block:
B. Carotid stenting is an alternative to endarterectomy for significant symptomatic stenosis in patients at high surgical risk; it is not indicated for 48%.
C. Carotid thrombectomy is not a standard treatment for carotid stenosis; mechanical thrombectomy is for an acute large-vessel intracranial occlusion in a current stroke.
D. Endarterectomy is right for symptomatic stenosis of 70 to 99% (and selected 50 to 69%), ideally within 2 weeks of the TIA; 48% is below the threshold.
key_concept:
Symptomatic carotid stenosis: the percentage decides.
  • Under 50%: medical therapy only (antiplatelet, statin, risk factors)
  • 50 to 69%: endarterectomy in selected patients
  • 70 to 99%: endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks
  • Complete occlusion: no surgery
  • Initial imaging after TIA: carotid duplex
exam_pearl: Change the number to 70% or more and the answer flips to carotid endarterectomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original typed recall: pt with HTN, dyslipidemia came with TIA for 30 minutes, Echo: carotid stenosis 48%; options Observe / Carotid endarterectomy / Carotid Stent; Observe highlighted.

stem: long scenario about an elderly who had colectomy, and post operation he had dehydration and increased skin turgor with postural hypotension. ABG results: PH 7.8 (high) HCO3 48 (high) PCO2 44 (high) PO2 (low) What is your interpretation?
why_right: The pH is high with a high HCO3 (48), so the primary disorder is metabolic alkalosis, from loss of gastric acid and volume after colectomy (dehydration, postural hypotension). Respiratory compensation would raise PCO2 well above normal (expected roughly 0.7 × HCO3 + 21, about 55); a PCO2 of 44 is essentially normal, so no meaningful compensation has occurred and the pH remains markedly raised. This recall's key is therefore uncompensated metabolic alkalosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. The word 'compensated' does not fit a pH this high, and neither disorder is compensating the other. Strictly, a PCO2 well below the expected value would mean a second, respiratory alkalosis, but exam keys read a normal PCO2 as no compensation.
C. Respiratory alkalosis is the primary problem only when PCO2 is low and HCO3 falls to compensate; here HCO3 is high and PCO2 is not low.
D. Respiratory compensation would show a clearly raised PCO2 near the expected value; a PCO2 of 44 is too close to normal to call compensation.
key_concept:
ABG reading in three steps.
  • pH: high = alkalosis, low = acidosis
  • Which value moves the same way as pH: HCO3 up with pH up = metabolic alkalosis
  • Compensation for metabolic alkalosis: PCO2 rises, expected about 0.7 × HCO3 + 21
  • PCO2 near normal = uncompensated
  • Vomiting or NG loss = HCl loss = hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
exam_pearl: Compare the actual PCO2 with the expected one: normal PCO2 with high HCO3 means no compensation yet.

stem: A previously healthy 55-year-old man undergoes elective right hemicolectomy for a stage I (T2N0M0) cancer of the cecum. His postoperative ileus is somewhat prolonged, and on the fifth postoperative day his nasogastric tube is still in place. Physical examination reveals diminished skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, and orthostatic hypotension. Pertinent laboratory values are as follows: What is the patient’s acid–base abnormality?
highlight_terms_source: nasogastric tube is still in place
