diminished skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, and orthostatic hypotension
why_right: Prolonged ileus with the nasogastric tube still in place on day 5 means continuous loss of gastric HCl, and the patient is volume depleted (poor skin turgor, dry mucosa, orthostatic hypotension). This produces a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis maintained by volume depletion. The lungs respond by hypoventilating, so PCO2 rises: metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation. The laboratory values were not preserved in the recall, so the clinical setting is the decisive clue.
why_wrong_block:
A. Uncompensated means PCO2 stays normal; respiratory compensation develops within hours, so by day 5 some rise in PCO2 is expected.
B. Respiratory acidosis needs hypoventilation as the primary problem (for example COPD or sedation), with low pH; NG loss gives a high pH from a metabolic cause.
C. A combined metabolic and respiratory alkalosis would need a low PCO2 from a second cause such as pain, sepsis or anxiety driving hyperventilation; nothing here suggests that.
key_concept:
GI losses decide the acid-base disorder.
  • Vomiting or NG suction: HCl loss = metabolic alkalosis (low Cl, low K)
  • Diarrhea: HCO3 and K loss = hypokalemic metabolic acidosis
  • Compensation of metabolic alkalosis: hypoventilation, PCO2 rises
  • Treatment: normal saline plus potassium
  • Compensation cannot be confirmed without an ABG or VBG
exam_pearl: NG tube or vomiting = alkalosis; diarrhea = acidosis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Laboratory values not included in the recall.

stem: Pediatric patient with recurrent UTI. Mother says she does not remember if any investigations were done. Came with dysuria, Investigations showed positive nitrate, leukocytes. What is the most indicated investigation?
why_right: The key clue is "recurrent UTI" with no record of prior imaging. Recurrent UTI raises concern for an underlying anatomical problem, especially vesicoureteral reflux or obstruction, so the child needs both a renal (and bladder) ultrasound to look at structure and hydronephrosis and a voiding cystourethrogram to detect reflux. Neither test alone answers both questions.
why_wrong_block:
A. VCUG alone shows reflux and urethral anatomy but misses hydronephrosis, renal size and structural anomalies that ultrasound detects; in recurrent UTI both are needed.
B. Renal ultrasound alone is the work-up after a first febrile UTI; with recurrent infections it cannot exclude reflux, so VCUG must be added.
D. KUB ultrasound is essentially the same structural scan as renal ultrasound and does not assess reflux, so it is incomplete for recurrent UTI.
key_concept:
Pediatric UTI imaging ladder.
  • First febrile UTI (infant): renal and bladder ultrasound
  • Abnormal ultrasound or recurrent UTI: add VCUG
  • DMSA: renal scarring, done later, not acutely
  • Do VCUG once the infection is treated
  • Risk factors: VUR, posterior urethral valves, constipation, uncircumcised male, incomplete emptying
exam_pearl: "First" UTI = ultrasound only; "recurrent" UTI = ultrasound plus VCUG.

stem: Child, I think six month, diagnosed with UTI, parent ask for further assessment, which of the following initial?
why_right: In a "six month" old with a diagnosed UTI, the lead-in asks for the "initial" further assessment. Renal and bladder ultrasound is the first imaging study: it is non-invasive, radiation-free and detects hydronephrosis, obstruction and congenital anomalies. Further tests are chosen based on the ultrasound result and whether UTIs recur.
why_wrong_block:
A. DMSA scan detects renal scarring; it is done months after the acute infection in atypical or recurrent UTI, not as the initial study.
C. CT abdomen gives radiation and adds nothing for routine pediatric UTI evaluation; it is kept for complications such as suspected abscess when ultrasound is inconclusive.
D. MCUG (VCUG) is invasive and needs catheterization; it is indicated after an abnormal ultrasound or recurrent febrile UTI, not first line.
key_concept:
Initial imaging after pediatric UTI = renal and bladder ultrasound.
  • Ultrasound: structure, hydronephrosis, obstruction
  • MCUG/VCUG: reflux; if ultrasound abnormal or UTI recurs
  • DMSA: scarring; delayed, selected cases
  • CT: not part of routine work-up in children
exam_pearl: "Initial" in a child with UTI almost always means ultrasound; MCUG is the trap.

stem: 4 years old complaining of recurrent infections ( 6 sinopulmonary and recurrent gastroenteritis and more than 4 giardiasis upon and his brother died 5 months due to sepsis upon examination all lymph nodes are not palpable Which of the following is the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: all lymph nodes are not palpable
why_right: A boy with recurrent "sinopulmonary" infections, recurrent gastroenteritis and repeated "giardiasis", a "brother died" of sepsis, and non-palpable lymph nodes fits X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia. A BTK defect blocks B cell maturation, so all immunoglobulin classes are low and lymphoid tissue (nodes, tonsils) is scant. Encapsulated bacterial sinopulmonary infections and Giardia are classic, and an affected male sibling points to X-linked inheritance.
why_wrong_block:
A. Omenn syndrome is a SCID variant of early infancy with erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and eosinophilia; here the nodes are absent and the child is 4.
B. This option was not recalled; any other immunodeficiency would need features this stem lacks (eczema and low platelets for Wiskott-Aldrich, normal or high IgM for hyper-IgM, later onset for CVID).
D. SCID presents in the first months with failure to thrive and opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, candida, severe viral) and is usually fatal early without transplant; a 4-year-old with mainly bacterial and Giardia infections fits a B cell defect.
key_concept:
Humoral (B cell) defect: bacterial sinopulmonary infections + Giardia, onset after maternal IgG wanes.
  • XLA: boys, all Ig low, B cells absent, T cells normal, tiny tonsils and nodes
  • SCID: early infancy, opportunistic infections, T and B both affected
  • Omenn: SCID with erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia
  • Wiskott-Aldrich: eczema, thrombocytopenia, infections
  • Hyper-IgM: CD40L defect, IgM normal or high
  • No live vaccines in suspected primary immunodeficiency
exam_pearl: Absent lymph nodes alone do not separate XLA from SCID; the age, bacterial plus Giardia pattern and male sibling point to XLA.

stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with recurrent pneumonia, chronic diarrhea, and otitis media. Laboratory evaluation reveals normal T-cell counts and undetectable levels of IgG, IgM, and IgA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: undetectable levels of IgG, IgM, and IgA
why_right: The decisive lab pattern is "normal T-cell counts" with "undetectable" IgG, IgM and IgA. A pure failure of antibody production with intact T cells is X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia, caused by a BTK defect that stops B cell maturation. Recurrent pneumonia and otitis media from encapsulated bacteria starting around 6 months, as maternal IgG wanes, is the classic timing.
why_wrong_block: A. SCID requires profoundly low or absent T cells (combined defect) with opportunistic infections; normal T-cell counts exclude it.
key_concept:
Read the T cells first.
  • All Ig low + T cells normal + B cells absent: XLA
  • T cells low + Ig low: SCID
  • IgM normal/high, IgG and IgA low: hyper-IgM (CD40L)
  • Onset around 6 months: maternal IgG protection fades
exam_pearl: Normal T cells rule out SCID no matter how sick or young the infant is.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: version within the 659 block, printed at the top of the next page.

stem: 45-year-old man with recurrent episodes of schizophrenia is on maintenance therapy to maintain suppression of symptoms, prevent relapse, improve quality of life, and support engagement in psychosocial therapy. Which of the following is the best outcome following the maintenance therapy?
OptC: 70% will have a satisfactory quality of life
why_right: Long-term outcome in schizophrenia follows the rule of thirds: about one third achieve lasting symptom reduction and good function, one third have a relapsing course with partial recovery, and one third remain chronically impaired. So even with good maintenance therapy, the best realistic outcome stated here is that about 33% obtain long-lasting symptom reduction.
why_wrong_block:
A. Complete resolution is not the expected outcome of maintenance therapy; its goals are symptom suppression and relapse prevention, and most patients keep some residual symptoms.
B. 5% understates outcomes; roughly a third do well, so remission is far more common than this.
C. 70% with satisfactory quality of life overstates outcomes; only about a third do well in the long term, and the rest have relapses or chronic impairment.
key_concept:
Schizophrenia prognosis, rule of thirds.
  • About one third: lasting improvement
  • About one third: relapsing course, partial recovery
  • About one third: chronic, severe impairment
  • Good prognosis: acute onset, late onset, clear trigger, positive symptoms, mood symptoms, good premorbid function, female sex, social support
  • Stopping maintenance antipsychotics sharply raises relapse risk
exam_pearl: Schizophrenia outcome questions: think in thirds, not cure.

stem: thyroid case TSH normal Ultrasound : 4×4 cm Besthesda classified = 0 FNA done but Inaccurate What the next?
why_right: With a normal TSH the nodule is not hot, so the pathway is ultrasound then FNA. The FNA was inadequate (Bethesda category 1, nondiagnostic), which gives no information on benign versus malignant. A nondiagnostic FNA is repeated, ideally under ultrasound guidance, before any decision on surgery.
why_wrong_block:
A. A thyroid scan is used when TSH is low, to look for a hot autonomous nodule; with a normal TSH it does not replace cytology.
C. Total thyroidectomy is for confirmed malignancy (Bethesda 6) or other clear indications; operating without a cytological diagnosis is premature. Persistently nondiagnostic results on repeat FNA may then lead to diagnostic surgery.
key_concept:
Bethesda result drives the next step.
  • 1 Nondiagnostic: repeat FNA (US guided)
  • 2 Benign: ultrasound follow up
  • 3 Atypia of undetermined significance: repeat FNA
  • 4 Follicular neoplasm: hemithyroidectomy
  • 5 Suspicious for malignancy: manage as 4 or 6
  • 6 Malignant: total (near total) thyroidectomy
exam_pearl: Low TSH sends you to a scan; normal TSH with a failed FNA sends you back to FNA.

stem: A 55-year-old man known to have psychiatric disease and hypertension was admitted to the hospital due to poor nutrition at home, as he was refusing food. During hospitalization, he became agitated, so they increased the dose of Haloperidol. Suddenly, he became confused and began sweating. He was shifted to the ICU, started on IV fluids, and intubated (see lab result). Which of the following should be added to the management plan?
why_right: Haloperidol is a potent dopamine antagonist, and the dose was increased just before he suddenly became confused and began sweating, needing ICU care and intubation. This is neuroleptic malignant syndrome: hyperthermia, rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability, usually with a markedly raised CK on labs. Beyond stopping the antipsychotic, cooling and IV fluids, the specific drug therapy is a dopamine agonist, bromocriptine (dantrolene is the other option).
why_wrong_block:
A. Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity (pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, coma); there is no opioid exposure and sweating is not an opioid feature.
B. Glucagon is the antidote for beta blocker (or calcium channel blocker) overdose and treats hypoglycemia; it has no role in NMS.
C. Meropenem is for severe bacterial sepsis; the confusion and sweating here follow the haloperidol dose increase and are drug induced, not infection, although sepsis should be excluded.
key_concept:
NMS = dopamine blockade → treat with dopamine agonist.
  • Triggers: antipsychotics (haloperidol), metoclopramide, abrupt stop of levodopa
  • Features: lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, confusion, autonomic instability
  • Labs: high CK, leukocytosis, possible myoglobinuria / AKI
  • Treat: stop drug, cooling, IV fluids, bromocriptine or dantrolene
  • Serotonin syndrome instead: clonus, hyperreflexia, rapid onset → cyproheptadine
exam_pearl: Antipsychotic + rigidity + fever + confusion = NMS (bromocriptine); SSRI + clonus = serotonin syndrome (cyproheptadine).

stem: A 32 years old female presented with severe pelvic pain and hypotension after MVA. CT: showed pelvic hematoma and active bleeding. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: pelvic pain and hypotension after MVA
why_right: After an MVA with severe pelvic pain, hypotension and a CT showing a pelvic hematoma with active bleeding, this is hemorrhagic shock from a pelvic (retroperitoneal) source. The priority is circulation: resuscitate with blood products (pRBCs, ideally balanced with plasma and platelets) and stabilize the pelvis with a binder, then control the bleeding by angioembolization or pelvic packing. Among the options, transfusion is the correct immediate management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Laparotomy is for intraperitoneal bleeding (for example positive FAST with instability); opening the abdomen does not control retroperitoneal pelvic bleeding and can release tamponade.
C. Crystalloid and observation suit a stable patient without active bleeding; a hypotensive patient with active extravasation needs blood, and large volumes of crystalloid worsen coagulopathy.
key_concept:
Hypotensive pelvic fracture: resuscitate, stabilize, embolize.
  • Blood products (massive transfusion protocol if needed)
  • Pelvic binder to reduce pelvic volume
  • Active arterial extravasation on CT: angioembolization
  • Alternative: preperitoneal pelvic packing or external fixation
  • Positive FAST and unstable: laparotomy for the abdominal source
exam_pearl: Blood in the pelvis is not fixed by a laparotomy; blood in the peritoneum is.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant recall (Q:): Female patient after MVA presented to the ED, hypotensive 90/50, CT showed pelvic hematoma and deep internal active bleed; options A. Blood transfusion (highlighted) / B. Ex. Lap.

stem: A child presented to the OPD with persistent purulent nasal discharge and low grade fever for 12 days. On examination: No periorbital swelling or restricted EOM. There is tenderness on the frontal bone. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: Purulent nasal discharge with fever persisting for 12 days (beyond 10 days without improvement) plus frontal tenderness meets the clinical definition of acute bacterial sinusitis. There are no complication signs (no periorbital swelling, EOM not restricted), so the child is managed as an outpatient with first line oral amoxicillin. Diagnosis is clinical; no imaging is needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Supportive care alone fits viral rhinosinusitis, which typically improves within about 10 days; symptoms persisting past 10 days indicate bacterial infection that warrants antibiotics.
C. Intranasal steroids are an adjunct (mainly in allergic or chronic rhinosinusitis) and do not replace antibiotics for acute bacterial sinusitis in a child.
D. Sinus X-ray is not recommended; uncomplicated sinusitis is a clinical diagnosis, and imaging (contrast CT) is reserved for suspected orbital or intracranial complications.
key_concept:
Acute bacterial sinusitis in children is a clinical diagnosis; treat with amoxicillin if criteria are met.
  • Persistent: nasal discharge or daytime cough >10 days without improvement
  • Severe onset: high fever with purulent discharge for 3 or more consecutive days
  • Worsening (double sickening): new worsening after initial improvement
  • First line: amoxicillin; no response by 72 h: amoxicillin clavulanate
  • Periorbital swelling, restricted EOM, proptosis or neuro signs: contrast CT plus IV antibiotics
exam_pearl: Under 10 days with improving symptoms is viral (supportive); once eye signs appear the answer flips to contrast CT.

stem: A patient presented to the ED after he was stabbed in his chest. Upon examination he had hypotension, tachycardia, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck veins. Lungs were clear bilaterally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A stab to the chest with hypotension, muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins is Beck's triad, and clear lungs bilaterally rule out a pneumothorax or hemothorax as the cause. Blood in the pericardial sac compresses the heart and limits filling, so the diagnosis is cardiac tamponade. It is confirmed by FAST or echo and treated by pericardiocentesis or surgical decompression when unstable.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myocardial contusion follows blunt trauma and presents with arrhythmias or a raised troponin, not muffled heart sounds after a stab wound.
B. Hemothorax causes hypotension with decreased breath sounds and dullness on one side, and the neck veins are usually flat from blood loss.
C. Tension pneumothorax also gives hypotension and raised JVP, but with absent breath sounds, hyperresonance and tracheal shift; the lungs here are clear.
key_concept:
Hypotension plus distended neck veins after chest trauma: listen to the lungs.
  • Clear equal breath sounds + muffled heart = tamponade
  • Absent breath sounds + hyperresonance + tracheal shift = tension pneumothorax
  • Dull side + flat neck veins = massive hemothorax
  • Tamponade extras: pulsus paradoxus, low-voltage ECG
  • Unstable tamponade: pericardiocentesis
exam_pearl: Raised JVP with hypotension is tamponade or tension pneumothorax; breath sounds separate them.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant recall (Q:): Patient with MVA came with muffled heart sound, BP 90/60. Diagnosis? A cardiac contusion / B. Pneumothorax / C. Cardiac tamponade / D. Heamothorax (no option marked).

stem: A pediatric patient in the PICU on mechanical ventilation due to sepsis-related respiratory failure. What can we do regarding mechanical ventilation to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury?
OptA: Zero positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to prevent barotrauma
OptB: Increase tidal volume with carbon dioxide reserve
OptD: Low tidal volume to maintain permissive hypercapnia
why_right: Lung-protective ventilation is the strategy to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury in a ventilated septic child with respiratory failure. Using low tidal volumes limits alveolar overdistension (volutrauma), and the resulting rise in CO2 is accepted as long as pH remains tolerable (permissive hypercapnia). This is the same principle that reduces mortality in adult ARDS, where tidal volume is set to about 6 mL/kg of predicted body weight.
why_wrong_block:
A. Zero PEEP lets alveoli collapse and reopen with each breath (atelectrauma) and worsens hypoxemia; removing PEEP does not prevent lung injury, and adequate PEEP is part of lung-protective ventilation.
B. Increasing tidal volume causes overdistension and volutrauma, the main mechanism of ventilator-induced lung injury.
C. Hyperventilation to wash out CO2 needs higher volumes or rates, increasing lung stress, and the hypocapnia causes alkalosis and cerebral vasoconstriction; it is not a protective strategy.
key_concept:
Lung-protective ventilation = low tidal volume + adequate PEEP + limited plateau pressure.
  • Volutrauma: high tidal volume
  • Barotrauma: high airway pressure
  • Atelectrauma: cyclic collapse with zero or low PEEP
  • Biotrauma: inflammatory mediators from injured lung
  • Accept higher CO2 (permissive hypercapnia) to keep volumes low
exam_pearl: "Washing out CO2" sounds safe but is the opposite of lung protection; tolerate the CO2, protect the alveoli.

stem: A child presents with periorbital eye swelling, hematuria, and hypertension 3 weeks after impetigo. ASO positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: periorbital eye swelling, hematuria, and hypertension
why_right: "Periorbital swelling, hematuria and hypertension" is a nephritic syndrome, and it follows a "sore throat 3 weeks ago" with a "positive ASO titre". This latent period of 1 to 3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis is classic for poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome in adults (heavy proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia), not post-infectious nephritic hematuria with hypertension.
B. IgA nephropathy gives hematuria within a few days of (or during) an upper respiratory infection; it would be right with a 1 to 2 day latency, not 3 weeks with a positive ASO.
key_concept:
Timing after infection separates the two classic causes.
  • PSGN: 1 to 3 weeks after throat (longer after skin) infection; positive ASO; low C3, normal C4
  • IgA nephropathy: hematuria within days of URTI; normal complement
  • Membranous: nephrotic, adults, anti-PLA2R
exam_pearl: Days after the sore throat = IgA nephropathy; weeks after = PSGN.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0477).

stem: An 8 year old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother. She is concerned of bed wetting overnight despite toilet training and compared to his sister when she was in his age with good control. Which of the following pelvic muscles is affected and possible target therapy?
why_right: An "8 year old" with nighttime bed wetting "despite toilet training" has primary nocturnal enuresis. One recognized mechanism is detrusor overactivity with reduced functional bladder capacity, and the detrusor is the muscle targeted by anticholinergic therapy (e.g. oxybutynin). The lead-in asks for the affected pelvic muscle and therapy target, which points to the detrusor.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rectus abdominis is an abdominal wall muscle with no role in bladder storage or voiding.
C. Perianal muscles (external anal sphincter) relate to fecal continence and encopresis, not nocturnal bladder control.
D. Pelvic floor dysfunction is linked to dysfunctional voiding with daytime symptoms; the classic muscle target in enuresis is the detrusor.
key_concept:
Enuresis mechanisms: nocturnal polyuria (low ADH), detrusor overactivity or small bladder capacity, impaired arousal from sleep.
  • Always do a urinalysis first
  • Primary (never dry) vs secondary (relapse after being dry): ask about stressors, UTI, diabetes
  • Treatment: behavioral measures and enuresis alarm, desmopressin for polyuria, anticholinergics for detrusor overactivity
  • Recurrent UTI: renal ultrasound + VCUG; spinal signs: MRI spine
  • Age cut off for diagnosis: 5 years in DSM-5/ICCS (some sources accept wetting as normal up to 6)
exam_pearl: Asked for a "muscle" in bed wetting: detrusor; asked for first line therapy: alarm or desmopressin.

stem: A 9-month-old infant has never received any vaccinations. What should be given at this visit?
OptD: BCG, Hep B, OPV-1, Dtap-1, Measles
why_right: A "9-month-old" who has "never received any vaccinations" needs catch-up immunization: give every vaccine he is eligible for at the same visit, starting with the missed earliest doses. That means the birth vaccines (BCG, Hep B), the first doses of the infant series (DTaP-1, polio) and the age-due measles dose. Option D is the most complete listed set.
why_wrong_block:
A. BCG and Hep B alone cover only the birth doses and miss DTaP, polio and the measles dose he is old enough for; delaying them wastes a vaccination opportunity.
B. This leaves out DTaP and polio, the core primary series; giving PCV while omitting DTaP and polio does not prioritize the essential missed vaccines.
C. This is close to the routine 9-month visit for a fully vaccinated child (measles + MCV4) plus DTaP and OPV, but it omits BCG and Hep B, which an unvaccinated child still needs.
key_concept:
Catch-up rule: never restart a series, give all due vaccines at one visit, then follow minimum intervals.
  • Saudi birth: BCG, Hep B
  • 2 and 4 months: IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV, rotavirus
  • 6 months: OPV, IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV
  • 9 months: measles + MCV4
  • 12 months: OPV, MMR, PCV, MCV4
  • Rotavirus is not started late in catch-up
exam_pearl: "Never vaccinated" means catch-up from birth doses plus whatever is due now, not just the vaccines of the current age.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant recall (Q:): Mother brought her 9-month child to well baby clinic, no previous vaccine; mother was vaccine-hesitant, then convinced: 'just give my child the necessary vaccination'. Options: A. DTaP, BCG / B. DTaP, BCG, IPV, OPV / C. DTaP, measles, BCG, Hep B, OPV (highlighted) / D. DTaP, measles, MCV 4, OPV.

stem: A full-term neonate boy presented with spontaneous soft tissue bleeding and joint swelling suggestive of hemarthrosis. Laboratory investigations showed a normal platelet count and a normal prothrombin time (PT), but the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) was prolonged. A mixing study was performed, and the aPTT failed to correct after mixing with normal plasma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
OptD: Maternal autoantibodies lead to acquired hemophilia
highlight_terms_source: aPTT failed to correct after mixing
why_right: A boy with hemarthrosis, normal platelets and PT, and an isolated prolonged aPTT points to the intrinsic pathway (VIII, IX, XI, XII). The decisive clue is that the aPTT failed to correct after mixing with normal plasma, which means an inhibitor (antibody) is present, not a factor deficiency. In a newborn, the source of such an inhibitor is maternal IgG anti factor VIII autoantibody crossing the placenta, causing a transient acquired hemophilia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Factor VIII deficiency also gives an isolated prolonged aPTT with hemarthrosis, but normal plasma supplies the missing factor, so the aPTT corrects on mixing. Right when the mixing study corrects.
B. Bernard Soulier syndrome is a platelet adhesion defect (GpIb) with large platelets, often low counts and mucocutaneous bleeding; PT and aPTT are normal and joint bleeds are not typical.
C. Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia causes petechiae and intracranial bleeding with a LOW platelet count; coagulation times are normal. Here platelets are normal.
key_concept:
Isolated prolonged aPTT: mixing study separates deficiency from inhibitor.
  • Corrects on mixing: factor deficiency (VIII, IX, XI, XII)
  • Fails to correct: inhibitor (factor VIII antibody, lupus anticoagulant)
  • Neonate with inhibitor: think maternal autoantibody crossing the placenta
  • Isolated PT: factor VII; both PT and aPTT: common pathway, vitamin K, liver
  • Low platelets + normal clotting: ITP, NAIT
exam_pearl: Same labs, but the aPTT corrects on mixing: the answer becomes factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A).

stem: A 75 year old female K/C of Afib and recent unintentional weight loss, presented to the ER with severe abdominal pain that is described as out of proportion, on examination the abdomen was soft but tender with decreased bowel sound.
why_right: An elderly woman with atrial fibrillation (embolic source) and pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen is acute mesenteric ischemia until proven otherwise; recent weight loss may reflect chronic intestinal ischemia (food fear). CT angiography is the test of choice: it is fast, shows the embolus or thrombus and the state of the bowel, and guides revascularization. It should not be delayed for other tests.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lactate supports ischemia but is nonspecific and may be normal early; a normal lactate does not exclude mesenteric ischemia.
B. Plain X-ray is usually normal early and only shows late signs (pneumatosis, free air); it is the first test for obstruction or perforation.
C. Ultrasound is limited by bowel gas and cannot reliably assess the mesenteric vessels in an acute abdomen; it is the first test for biliary pain.
key_concept:
Acute mesenteric ischemia: suspect clinically, confirm with CT angiography.
  • Risk: AF, recent MI, valve disease, elderly with vascular disease
  • Hallmark: severe pain, benign abdomen
  • Late: bloody diarrhea, peritonitis, lactic acidosis
  • Test of choice: CT angiography
  • Treatment: heparin, revascularization, resect dead bowel
exam_pearl: AF plus pain out of proportion to examination = mesenteric ischemia = CT angiography.

stem: A 4-week-old infant presents with projectile, non-bilious vomiting that frequently contains clotted milk. After vomiting, the child still seems to be hungry. Which of the following is the appropriate diagnostic test?
why_right: A 4 week old with projectile, non bilious vomiting who is still hungry afterwards is classic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Abdominal ultrasound is the first and diagnostic investigation: it shows a thickened, elongated pyloric muscle, is noninvasive and involves no radiation. Whether the lead in says initial, next or most appropriate, the answer for suspected pyloric stenosis is ultrasound.
why_wrong_block:
A. Abdominal X ray may show a single bubble (distended stomach) but cannot measure the pylorus or confirm the diagnosis; it is not the test of choice.
B. Upper endoscopy is invasive, needs anesthesia and is not used to diagnose pyloric stenosis; it is for mucosal disease such as esophagitis or ulcers.
key_concept:
Pyloric stenosis: projectile non bilious vomiting at 2 to 8 weeks, hungry after vomiting.
  • Exam: olive shaped mass in RUQ / epigastrium, visible peristalsis
  • Labs: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
  • Diagnosis: abdominal ultrasound
  • Bilious vomiting instead: upper GI contrast study (malrotation)
  • Treatment: correct fluids and electrolytes first, then pyloromyotomy
exam_pearl: Bilious vomiting flips the answer to an upper GI contrast study to exclude malrotation with volvulus.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant (Q:): child with non-bilious vomiting, hungry after vomiting, visible peristalsis; most appropriate investigation: stool culture / abdominal X-ray / upper GI endoscopy / Abdominal Ultrasound (highlighted). Screenshot: 1-month-old, palpable 'olive' in RUQ, initial imaging: CT / MRI / Upper GI series / **D. Ultrasound abdomen. Note: Abdominal Ultrasound (next or most appropriate, all are same for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis). If there is BILIOUS vomiting: Upper GI contrast study.

stem: A patient with history of chronic intermittent claudication presented with sudden onset of acute limb ischemia. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test?
highlight_terms_source: sudden onset of acute limb ischemia
why_right: Sudden limb ischemia on a background of chronic claudication is acute-on-chronic ischemia, usually thrombosis on an atherosclerotic plaque. The lead-in asks for the initial diagnostic test: bedside Doppler ultrasound assesses arterial and venous signals, grades the threat to the limb and localizes the occlusion, and it is done after heparin is started. CT angiography follows as the confirmatory test if the limb is not immediately threatened.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT angiography is the confirmatory (most appropriate) test for planning revascularization, not the initial bedside test; with paralysis, imaging is skipped altogether.
C. ABI is the first test for chronic peripheral arterial disease (claudication), not for an acute ischemic limb, where Doppler signals guide urgency.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia ladder: heparin, Doppler, CT angiography.
  • 6 Ps: pain, pallor, paresthesia, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis
  • Initial test: Doppler ultrasound
  • Confirmatory: CT angiography
  • Paralysis or motor loss: skip imaging, go to theatre
  • Embolic (AF): embolectomy; thrombotic: catheter-directed thrombolysis or bypass
  • Chronic PAD: ABI first
exam_pearl: 'Initial' test = Doppler; 'most appropriate' or confirmatory test = CT angiography.

stem: A child with liver cirrhosis due to autoimmune hepatitis, what food should he avoid?
why_right: This recall's key is fat because, in chronic liver disease, reduced bile salt secretion impairs fat digestion and absorption, so a high fat intake worsens steatorrhea and malabsorption symptoms. The recall rule is: liver cirrhosis or autoimmune hepatitis without encephalopathy, limit fat. Protein is not restricted in this setting because the child needs it for growth and to prevent muscle wasting.
why_wrong_block:
A. Protein is needed for growth in a child with cirrhosis; restriction was older teaching reserved for hepatic encephalopathy, which is not described here.
B. Carbohydrates are the main energy source and are encouraged to meet the high calorie needs of cirrhosis; they are not avoided.
D. Minerals and vitamins (especially fat soluble A, D, E, K) are supplemented in chronic liver disease, not avoided.
key_concept:
Nutrition in pediatric chronic liver disease: high calorie, adequate protein, supplement vitamins.
  • Fat: reduced bile flow causes malabsorption and steatorrhea (keyed answer)
  • Protein: maintain; old teaching restricted only with encephalopathy
  • Carbohydrate: main calorie source
  • Fat soluble vitamins A, D, E, K: supplement
  • Ascites: salt restriction
exam_pearl: If the stem adds hepatic encephalopathy, older exam recalls switch the answer to protein.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Hepatitis/liver cirrhosis/autoimmune hepatitis without encephalopathy = fat (compiler's note).

stem: Long term management of X-linked Severe combined immunodeficiency?
why_right: X linked SCID (common gamma chain defect) leaves the child without functioning T cells, and B cells do not work properly either. The only curative, long term treatment is hematopoietic stem cell (bone marrow) transplant, ideally early in infancy before serious infections; gene therapy is an emerging alternative in specialised centres.
why_wrong_block: B. Monthly immunoglobulin replacement only covers the antibody defect and is a supportive bridge until transplant; it does not restore T cell immunity. It is the long term treatment for pure antibody defects such as X linked agammaglobulinemia.
key_concept:
SCID: absent T cell function; fatal in infancy without transplant.
  • Definitive: hematopoietic stem cell transplant
  • Bridge: IVIG, PJP prophylaxis, antimicrobial prophylaxis
  • Avoid live vaccines (BCG, rotavirus)
  • Use irradiated, CMV negative blood products
  • X linked agammaglobulinemia: lifelong IVIG instead
exam_pearl: Pure B cell defect (X linked agammaglobulinemia) flips the answer to lifelong immunoglobulin replacement.

stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C present to the clinic for regular follow-up. His examination reveals a palpable right upper quadrant mass. CT scan of his abdomen shows a large 6*6 cm mass in the right lobe of the liver. A mass biopsy confirms the diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma. What is the most appropriate management steps at this stage?
why_right: A single 6 × 6 cm biopsy-proven HCC confined to the right lobe, in a patient attending routine follow-up with no stated decompensation or metastasis, is localized and potentially curable. A solitary tumour with preserved liver function is treated by resection. Some exam keys favour TACE for a single lesion of 6 cm or more; TACE is not offered, so referral for surgical resection is the answer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Systemic therapy is reserved for advanced HCC (vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread); conventional chemotherapy has little role in localized disease.
B. Radiotherapy is not the standard primary treatment of a resectable HCC; it is used selectively when other locoregional options are not possible.
C. Palliative care alone is for end-stage disease (poor performance status or decompensated cirrhosis); this tumour is localized and treatable.
key_concept:
HCC treatment by burden and liver function.
  • Single tumour, preserved liver function: surgical resection
  • Small tumours within transplant criteria with cirrhosis: transplant or ablation
  • Multiple or large unresectable lesions: TACE
  • Vascular invasion or metastasis: systemic therapy
  • End-stage: supportive care
exam_pearl: If TACE is listed for a large or multifocal HCC, it may be the key; if not, choose resection.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant recall (Q:): 4×4 hepatocellular carcinoma management? A. chemotherapy / B. Radiotherapy / C. Surgery (highlighted).

stem: A child presents with symptoms of celiac disease and has positive anti-tTG IgA and positive anti-endomysial antibody (EMA). Which of the following is considered the definitive diagnostic test?
why_right: Positive anti tTG IgA and anti endomysial antibody make celiac disease very likely, but serology is the initial screening step. The lead in asks for the definitive diagnostic test, which is upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes. The child must remain on gluten until the biopsy to avoid a false negative result.
why_wrong_block:
A. Positive serology alone is not the definitive test here; no stem detail (such as very high tTG levels confirmed on a second sample) supports skipping the biopsy.
C. HLA DQ2/DQ8 typing has a high negative predictive value and is used to rule celiac disease OUT in unclear cases; a positive result does not confirm it.
D. Repeating serology in 6 months delays diagnosis; repeat serology is used to monitor adherence once the child is on a gluten free diet.
key_concept:
Celiac disease: serology screens, duodenal biopsy confirms.
  • Initial: IgA anti tTG (with total IgA level)
  • Confirm: endoscopy with duodenal biopsy
  • Keep eating gluten before testing
  • HLA DQ2/DQ8: rule out, not rule in
  • Follow up adherence: tTG levels
  • Treatment: lifelong gluten free diet
exam_pearl: Pediatric guidelines allow a no biopsy diagnosis when tTG IgA is at least 10 times the upper limit and EMA is positive on a second sample; a stem giving those details could make no further testing correct.

stem: A baby with hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia was diagnosed with congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21 hydroxylase deficiency. What is the most appropriate next step ?
OptB: IV hydrocortisone and isotonic normal saline
highlight_terms_source: congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21 hydroxylase deficiency
why_right: Hypoglycemia, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia in a baby with 21 hydroxylase deficiency is a salt wasting adrenal crisis: cortisol and aldosterone are both lacking. The immediate step is IV stress dose hydrocortisone with an isotonic normal saline bolus to restore volume and sodium; hydrocortisone also lowers potassium and raises glucose. IV dextrose is added for the hypoglycemia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone is the long term maintenance regimen once the baby is stable; it is too slow and unreliable in an acute crisis.
C. Sodium bicarbonate and insulin only shift potassium temporarily, do not treat the cortisol and aldosterone deficiency, and insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia.
key_concept:
Salt wasting CAH crisis: hydrocortisone + saline bolus + dextrose if hypoglycemic.
  • Typical age: 1 to 3 weeks with vomiting, dehydration
  • Labs: low Na, high K, low glucose, acidosis, high 17 OHP
  • Acute: IV hydrocortisone, 0.9% saline, IV dextrose
  • Maintenance: oral hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone (+ salt in infants)
  • Inheritance: autosomal recessive
exam_pearl: Stable child or asking about long term therapy: the answer becomes oral hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant recall (Q:): child with 21-hydroxylase CAH (diagnosis was written) with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis; initial management: A. Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone / B. IV fluids and IV hydrocortisone (highlighted).

stem: A 6 years old boy came to the clinic with ecchymosis post viral URTI two weeks ago. He has no hepatosplenomegaly. Labs showed low platelets. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: ecchymosis post viral URTI two weeks ago
why_right: Bruising 2 weeks after a viral URTI in a well child with no hepatosplenomegaly and low platelets is classic immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). Once the CBC shows isolated thrombocytopenia, the peripheral blood film confirms it: large platelets with otherwise normal red and white cells, excluding platelet clumping, blasts and red cell fragmentation. ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion that rests on CBC plus film.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coagulation profile is normal in ITP, so it does not confirm the diagnosis; it helps when a clotting disorder or DIC is suspected.
B. Bone marrow aspirate is reserved for atypical features (another cytopenia, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone pain, blasts) or failure to respond to treatment, where leukemia or aplasia must be excluded.
key_concept:
Pediatric ITP: isolated thrombocytopenia after a viral illness in a well child.
  • Initial: CBC
  • Confirm / next after CBC: peripheral blood film
  • Two or more cell lines low, organomegaly, bone pain: bone marrow aspirate
  • Marrow in ITP: increased megakaryocytes
  • Treat if significant bleeding: steroids or IVIG
exam_pearl: Add anemia, high WBC, bone pain or hepatosplenomegaly and the answer becomes bone marrow aspirate to exclude leukemia.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Isolated thrombocytopenia (ITP): Initial, Next, CONFIRM: CBC (if present), Blood film (if CBC already done or not present). 2 cell line defect (thrombocytopenia + anemia or neutropenia): Initial/Next (without the word 'confirm'): CBC > Blood film (debated approach); CONFIRM (e.g. initial to confirm or next to confirm): Bone marrow.

stem: 6 Y/O boy brought by his mother C/o fatigue and O/E hepatosplenomegaly labs showed WBC 2.5 Hb 8 also plt low what is the next step to confirm the diagnosis?
why_right: A 6 year old with fatigue, hepatosplenomegaly and low WBC, Hb and platelets has pancytopenia with organomegaly, which points to marrow infiltration such as leukemia. The lead in is confirm the diagnosis, and only bone marrow examination (aspirate and biopsy) establishes it and classifies the disease.
why_wrong_block: B. Blood film: a quick supportive step that may show blasts, but it cannot confirm or classify leukemia and may be blast free (aleukemic); it would be the answer if the question asked for the initial test.
key_concept:
Two or more cell lines down = bone marrow.
  • Pancytopenia + hepatosplenomegaly or lymph nodes: think leukemia, confirm by bone marrow
  • Pancytopenia without organomegaly: think aplastic anemia, also bone marrow
  • Isolated low platelets after viral illness: ITP, marrow not needed (increased megakaryocytes if done)
exam_pearl: Initial test = CBC and film; confirmatory test = bone marrow examination.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1363).
Compiler note: Screenshot note: It was 'Next To Confirm', not Next alone or 'Best Next' (the word 'Confirm' was present). Confirmed, 'A- Bone Marrow'.

stem: A term baby, born to a diabetic mother with respiratory distress and desatting. He is macrosomic. What is the next appropriate step?
OptA: Admit to NICU and monitor glucose
why_right: A macrosomic term infant of a diabetic mother with respiratory distress and desaturation is at risk of several problems at once: RDS (hyperinsulinemia delays surfactant), transient tachypnea, polycythemia, cardiomyopathy and especially hypoglycemia. The appropriate next step is NICU admission for oxygen support, close monitoring and serial glucose checks, escalating only if the baby deteriorates.
why_wrong_block:
B. Intubation and mechanical ventilation are for respiratory failure (apnea, severe distress or hypoxia despite oxygen or CPAP); the stem gives no such severity.
C. Immediate surfactant is not given before RDS is established and the baby is assessed; it is typically given via an endotracheal tube to a baby with confirmed RDS needing support.
D. Empirical antibiotics are right when there are sepsis risk factors (maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, GBS); none are given here, and the stem's emphasis is the diabetic mother.
key_concept:
Infant of diabetic mother in distress: stabilise airway and breathing in NICU and check glucose early.
  • Hypoglycemia from fetal hyperinsulinemia
  • RDS even at term (surfactant delay), TTN
  • Polycythemia, hyperbilirubinemia, hypocalcemia
  • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
  • Macrosomia: shoulder dystocia, Erb palsy
exam_pearl: If the stem shows apnea or severe hypoxia despite oxygen, the answer moves to airway support and ventilation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant (Q:): newborn of diabetic mother, respiratory distress and desaturation shortly after birth, macrosomia (Examiner 1: just desatting, no numbers; Examiner 2: sat in 80s); B. NICU admission, glucose monitoring, and observation highlighted. Another variant: post-term/full-term macrosomic baby of DM/GDM mother with MAS, respiratory distress and de-sating, no numbers: 1. Intubation and ventilation / 2. NICU admission and glucose monitoring / 3. wait and reassess (unmarked).

stem: A 2-month-old premature infant born at 28 weeks gestation required CPAP and supplemental oxygen for 2 months. When transitioned to nasal cannula, the infant develops a monophasic expiratory wheeze. What is the most likely diagnosis?
OptB: Tracheomalacia due to prolonged airway support/intubation
why_right: A 28 week preterm infant who needed CPAP for 2 months and now has a monophasic expiratory wheeze has acquired tracheomalacia: prolonged positive pressure and intubation damage the immature tracheal cartilage, so the trachea collapses during expiration. A single pitched (monophasic) wheeze comes from one large central airway, unlike the diffuse polyphonic wheeze of small airway disease. Diagnosis is by bronchoscopy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is chronic lung disease of prematurity (oxygen need at 36 weeks corrected age) with tachypnea, retractions and diffuse polyphonic wheeze; it does not explain a fixed monophasic central wheeze.
C. Congenital subglottic stenosis is present from birth and causes biphasic or inspiratory stridor and recurrent croup; an ACQUIRED stenosis after intubation is possible but still gives stridor, not expiratory wheeze.
D. Laryngomalacia causes INSPIRATORY stridor from early weeks, worse supine and better prone; it is not related to ventilation and does not cause expiratory wheeze.
key_concept:
Noisy breathing in infants: phase and pitch localize the lesion.
  • Inspiratory stridor: laryngeal (laryngomalacia)
  • Biphasic stridor: subglottic or tracheal fixed narrowing
  • Monophasic expiratory wheeze: intrathoracic large airway (tracheomalacia)
  • Polyphonic wheeze: small airways (BPD, bronchiolitis, asthma)
  • Tracheomalacia: bronchoscopy; laryngomalacia: laryngoscopy
exam_pearl: Inspiratory stridor worse supine since early infancy, with no ventilation history: the answer becomes laryngomalacia.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same question shown twice. Numbered 707: infant born at 28 weeks on BIPAP for 2 months, off bipap developed monophasic wheeze; only A. Laryngomalacia / B. Tracheomalacia due to prolonged intubation (highlighted). Fuller 'Q:' version used here, also highlighting tracheomalacia.

stem: Young female with history of lack of sleep, decreased appetite, decreased concentration, loss of interest in activities and isolation. Which of the following is the most concerning?
OptA: Loss of interest in previously interesting activity
why_right: This young woman has depressive symptoms, and most concerning means the feature that most raises suicide risk. Isolation and social withdrawal (lack of social support) is an established suicide risk factor in depression, while the other options are core depressive symptoms that confirm the diagnosis but carry less risk on their own.
why_wrong_block:
A. Loss of interest (anhedonia) is a core symptom that helps diagnose depression, but it is not singled out as a suicide risk marker the way isolation is.
C. Changes in appetite and sleep are neurovegetative features of depression; they support the diagnosis but are not the most concerning risk feature.
D. Decreased concentration is a common depressive symptom affecting function but does not by itself signal high suicide risk.
key_concept:
Most concerning in depression = the feature that raises suicide risk; social isolation tops these options.
  • SAD PERSONS: Sex male, Age (young or elderly), Depression, Previous attempt, Ethanol or drugs, Rational thinking lost, Social support lacking, Organised plan, No spouse, Sickness
  • Women attempt more, men complete more
  • Always ask directly about suicidal thoughts
exam_pearl: If an option names a plan, previous attempt or suicidal thoughts, that outranks isolation.

stem: A 27 year old lady complaining of dysmenorrhea during menstruation. Now she start complaining of irritability, insomnia and suicidal thoughts thet start before menstruation by 5 days. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: Mood symptoms (irritability, insomnia) that start about 5 days before menstruation are tied to the luteal phase. When the affective symptoms are severe, here suicidal thoughts, the diagnosis is premenstrual dysphoric disorder, the severe mood-dominant form of PMS. The dysmenorrhea is incidental.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bipolar disorder has manic or hypomanic episodes lasting days to weeks not linked to the cycle; here symptoms recur only before menses.
B. Generalised anxiety disorder is excessive worry on most days for at least 6 months, not cyclic premenstrual symptoms.
C. Perimenopausal depression occurs near menopause (usually mid-40s or later) with irregular cycles and vasomotor symptoms; she is 27.
key_concept:
Luteal-phase symptoms that resolve with menses: PMS if mild to moderate, PMDD if mood symptoms are severe.
  • Onset in the week before menses, resolves within the first few days of menses
  • PMDD: marked irritability, depression, anxiety or lability with functional impairment
  • Clinical diagnosis, confirmed by a prospective symptom diary over 2 cycles
  • Treatment: lifestyle, then SSRI (best evidence), then combined OCP
exam_pearl: Timing makes the diagnosis: symptoms confined to the premenstrual week point to PMS or PMDD whatever the mood symptom.

stem: An elderly female with DM and HTN is scheduled for elective surgery. BP 160/95 Glucose 9.1 mmol/L What would you do?
OptA: Postpone her surgery for one month
OptB: Adjust her HTN and DM medications
why_right: The lead-in asks what you would do for an elective case in an elderly patient with DM and HTN whose readings are only moderately raised (BP 160/95, glucose 9.1 mmol/L). Neither value signals an active, decompensated problem, so the task is optimization: adjust her antihypertensive and diabetic regimen so she reaches surgery with controlled BP and glucose. Elective surgery is postponed only for decompensated or dangerous states (e.g. volume overload, recent MI, severe hypertension).
why_wrong_block:
A. Postponing for a month is reserved for decompensated conditions (heart failure with volume overload, recent MI, uncontrolled thyroid disease, severe hypertension); these mild elevations do not justify cancelling an elective case.
C. A routine preoperative chest X-ray has no role without cardiorespiratory symptoms or signs; it does not address the abnormal BP and glucose.
D. Baseline bloods (renal function, electrolytes) may well be checked in a diabetic hypertensive, but they are routine work-up, not the action this question targets; the abnormal findings presented are BP and glucose, which need treating.
key_concept:
Elective surgery: optimize controllable comorbidity; delay only for decompensated or high-risk states.
  • Mildly raised BP/glucose: adjust medications, proceed
  • Severe hypertension (≥180/110): defer and control first
  • Volume overload (raised JVP, crackles, edema): delay until optimized
  • Recent MI: delay elective noncardiac surgery (current guidance at least 60 days; older teaching 6 months)
  • Hypo/hyperthyroid: delay until euthyroid
  • Emergency surgery is never delayed for optimization
exam_pearl: Moderate, non-emergent abnormalities = optimize medications; only decompensation earns a postponement.

stem: A child complaining of constipations. On examination there was decreased anal sphincter tone and dilated rectum with fecal impaction. Family was asking how to prevent this from reoccurrence:
why_right: Reduced anal tone with a dilated rectum and fecal impaction describes chronic functional constipation with retention: the stretched rectum loses sensation and tone. This recall's key for preventing recurrence is good toilet habits: behavioral retraining with scheduled sitting after meals, a proper footrest and positive reinforcement, so the rectum is emptied regularly and can regain size and sensation.
why_wrong_block:
B. A high fiber diet is general advice, but extra fiber beyond normal age intake has little proven benefit and can increase bulk in an already overstretched rectum; it is not the key preventive step.
C. Long term laxatives (maintenance osmotic laxative such as PEG) are used after disimpaction to keep stools soft, but they are combined with, not a substitute for, toilet training in this recall.
key_concept:
Functional constipation with impaction: disimpact, maintain, retrain.
  • Disimpaction: oral PEG (or enemas)
  • Maintenance: osmotic laxative for months, wean slowly
  • Behavior: scheduled toileting after meals, diary, rewards
  • Diet: normal fiber and fluids
  • Hirschsprung contrast: empty rectum, tight sphincter, explosive stool on DRE
  • Lax anus with neuro signs: look for spinal cause
exam_pearl: If the question asks about the step right after disimpaction or drug therapy, the answer becomes a maintenance osmotic laxative.

stem: A child previously diagnosed with HSP presents with new-onset abdominal pain, bilateral ankle swelling, and hematuria with proteinuria on urinalysis. There is also a family history of SLE. What is the most likely cause of his current presentation?
OptA: Early nephritis due to systemic lupus erythematosus
OptC: Expected with HSP due to systemic vasculitis
why_right: The child already has a diagnosis of HSP (IgA vasculitis), and the new picture of abdominal pain, ankle swelling and hematuria with proteinuria is three of the four classic HSP features (purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, renal involvement), all from the same small vessel vasculitis. HSP nephritis typically appears within weeks to months of the rash, so these findings are expected disease manifestations rather than a new illness. The family history of SLE is a distractor; it does not outweigh an established, fitting diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lupus nephritis needs features of SLE in the child (malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, cytopenias, positive ANA/anti-dsDNA); a family history alone is not evidence, and HSP already explains the renal findings.
B. JIA is a chronic arthritis (≥6 weeks) with morning stiffness and does not cause hematuria, proteinuria or abdominal pain; the ankle swelling here is the HSP arthritis/edema.
D. UTI gives dysuria, fever and pyuria; significant proteinuria with hematuria points to a glomerular process, not infection.
key_concept:
HSP = palpable purpura (legs/buttocks, normal platelets) + arthritis/arthralgia + abdominal pain + renal involvement.
  • Renal: hematuria ± proteinuria; the main determinant of long term prognosis
  • Follow-up: serial urinalysis and BP for months after the episode
  • GI complication to watch: intussusception (usually ileo-ileal)
  • Lupus nephritis: needs systemic SLE features and serology
exam_pearl: A known HSP child with new renal findings has HSP nephritis until proven otherwise; a family history of SLE is a red herring.

stem: A 25 year old man presented to the Emergency Department after a motor vehicle accident. Initially he was stable then he lost consciousness. Dilated pupils were noted on examination. GCS was 8/15. CT brain shows convex hematoma in the temporal region. What is the appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: convex hematoma in the temporal region
why_right: "Initially stable then lost consciousness" is a lucid interval, and a convex (lens shaped) collection in the temporal region is an epidural hematoma from the middle meningeal artery. Dilated pupils and GCS 8 mean uncal herniation is under way. An expanding arterial bleed with herniation signs needs emergency craniotomy and evacuation; medical measures only buy minutes.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oxygenation is part of resuscitation (and a GCS of 8 needs a secured airway), but oxygen does not remove the expanding hematoma compressing the brain.
C. Steroids give no benefit in traumatic brain injury and are associated with harm; they help vasogenic edema around tumors, not traumatic bleeds.
D. A shunt treats hydrocephalus (CSF diversion), not an acute extra-axial hematoma causing herniation.
key_concept:
Epidural hematoma with deterioration = emergency craniotomy.
  • Epidural: convex/lens shaped, middle meningeal artery, lucid interval
  • Subdural: concave/crescent, bridging veins, elderly and alcoholics
  • Temporal fracture + lucid interval + ipsilateral blown pupil = epidural
  • Mannitol/hyperventilation: temporizing bridge only
  • GCS ≤8: secure the airway
exam_pearl: Mannitol or hyperventilation may appear as options, but once there is herniation from a surgical lesion the answer is to evacuate it (craniotomy).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): Patient presents by ambulance and was intubated; initially was conscious then became unresponsive; CT brain after resuscitation shows convex hematoma. A) Mannitol, B) Hyperventilation, C) Craniotomy [highlighted].

stem: A child had head trauma then went to sleep. When he woke up, he was drowsy and not fully alert. CT showed extracranial hemorrhage after trauma. What is the next step?
highlight_terms_source: head trauma then went to sleep
why_right: The child had head trauma, then "went to sleep" and woke drowsy and not fully alert. That is deterioration after an interval, the classic course of an expanding epidural (extradural) hematoma. With a confirmed post-traumatic bleed and a falling level of consciousness, the source keys immediate craniotomy to evacuate it before herniation occurs.
why_wrong_block:
B. Waiting while the conscious level is falling lets an expanding arterial bleed progress to herniation. Intubation protects the airway but does not treat the lesion.
C. MRI is slow and adds nothing once CT has shown the bleed; it is used for diffuse axonal injury or subtle lesions, not acute surgical hematomas.
D. Observation suits a small hematoma in a child who is fully alert with no neurological deficit; this child is already drowsy.
key_concept:
Post-traumatic intracranial bleed + declining consciousness = surgical evacuation.
  • Lucid interval then drowsiness: epidural hematoma until proven otherwise
  • Small hematoma, alert child, no deficit: observe with serial neuro checks
  • Any deterioration: neurosurgery now
  • CT is the imaging of choice in acute head trauma
exam_pearl: "Went to sleep then woke drowsy" is the lucid-interval story; don't let the vague wording push you to observe.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot inside block 718; 'A. Immediate craniotomy' printed at the bottom of the screenshot as the answer.

stem: A 45 year old woman presented to the Emergency Department after a motor vehicle accident with confusion, headache, and left-sided weakness. GCS is 14/15. CT brain showed a subdural hematoma. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: After an MVA she has a CT-proven subdural hematoma with left-sided weakness (a focal deficit from mass effect) and confusion. GCS 14 does not mean she is safe: a focal deficit shows the hematoma is compressing the brain. The next step is immediate neurosurgical involvement for evacuation, before she deteriorates further.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oxygen supports resuscitation but does nothing for a space-occupying hematoma; she is already maintaining a GCS of 14.
C. High-dose steroids are not used in head injury and are associated with worse outcomes; they suit tumor-related vasogenic edema.
key_concept:
Acute subdural hematoma: whether to operate depends on mass effect and neurological status, not GCS alone.
  • CT: concave/crescent collection, torn bridging veins
  • Thickness >10 mm or midline shift >5 mm: evacuate regardless of GCS
  • GCS falling by 2 or more points, or pupil asymmetry/fixed pupils: evacuate
  • Small, no shift, neurologically intact: observe with serial CT and neuro checks
  • Steroids: no role in traumatic brain injury
exam_pearl: A near-normal GCS with a new focal deficit still makes this a neurosurgical problem; the lateralizing sign outweighs the GCS.

stem: A 65 year old man presented to the Emergency Department with signs of lateralization and GCS 7/15. CT brain shows a 13 mm hematoma with midline shift. The patient was intubated and resuscitated. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: He has signs of lateralization, GCS 7, and a 13 mm hematoma with midline shift, which is significant mass effect. The airway is already secured (intubated and resuscitated), so the next step is definitive: emergency craniotomy and evacuation to relieve the compression.
why_wrong_block:
B. IV mannitol temporarily lowers ICP while theatre is prepared; it does not remove the clot, so it is a bridge, not the management.
C. ICU observation suits a small hematoma without shift in a neurologically stable patient, not a comatose patient with midline shift.
key_concept:
Mass effect + coma + lateralizing signs = evacuate.
  • ABC first: GCS ≤8, intubate
  • Temporizing ICP control: head up, mannitol/hypertonic saline, brief hyperventilation
  • Definitive: craniotomy and hematoma evacuation
  • Observation only for small lesions without shift in a stable patient
exam_pearl: "Intubated and resuscitated" tells you ABC is done; the remaining answer is surgery, not more medical ICP control.

stem: He has difficulty maintaining sleep for the last 3 months. His irregular sleep pattern was documented in his diary. I forgot the exact stem but it was like what is the most appropriate advise for his sleep health?
OptC: Regular sleep schedule and limit screen time
highlight_terms_source: difficulty maintaining sleep for the last 3 months
why_right: Difficulty maintaining sleep for 3 months, documented in a sleep diary, meets chronic insomnia disorder. First-line treatment for chronic insomnia is CBT for insomnia (stimulus control, sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, cognitive therapy), which works better long term than medication.
why_wrong_block:
B. Afternoon caffeine worsens sleep onset and maintenance; caffeine should be avoided later in the day.
C. A regular schedule and limiting screens are sleep hygiene, which is only one part of CBT-I and not enough alone for chronic insomnia; it is the answer when a behavioural cause is the whole problem without established chronic insomnia.
D. Sedative hypnotics are short-term adjuncts only, with tolerance, dependence and falls risk; they are not first line.
key_concept:
Chronic insomnia disorder (about 3 months, diary confirmed) = CBT-I first line.
  • CBT-I: stimulus control, sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, cognitive restructuring
  • Sleep hygiene alone: fine for simple behavioural sleep problems
  • Hypnotics: short term, lowest dose
  • Screen for depression, OSA, drugs and caffeine
exam_pearl: Duration flips the answer: about 3 months of insomnia means CBT-I, not just sleep hygiene advice.

stem: 25 y/o has difficulty with sleep, sleepy on afternoons. Work on his computer programming at night, has irregular sleep schedule. What to do?
OptB: Regular sleep schedule and limit screen time
highlight_terms_source: Work on his computer programming at night
why_right: A young programmer who works at night with an irregular sleep schedule and afternoon sleepiness has a behavioural and circadian problem driven by poor sleep hygiene and evening screen light. The first step is to correct the cause: fix a regular sleep and wake time and limit screen exposure before bed.
why_wrong_block: A. CBT for insomnia is first line for chronic insomnia disorder (difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep on most nights for about 3 months despite adequate opportunity); here the problem is a self-imposed irregular schedule, so simple sleep hygiene comes first.
key_concept:
Sleep complaint from an irregular, night-time, screen-heavy routine = fix sleep hygiene first.
  • Fixed wake time and bedtime, including weekends
  • Limit screens and bright light before bed
  • Avoid caffeine later in the day and long daytime naps
  • Chronic insomnia disorder (about 3 months) = CBT-I first line
  • Hypnotics are short term only, never first line
exam_pearl: Clear behavioural trigger (night work, irregular hours, screens) points to sleep hygiene; a documented chronic insomnia disorder points to CBT-I.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0285).

stem: A child with atopic dermatitis (eczema) has been treated with topical corticosteroids and emollients with minimal improvement. What is the best next step in management?
OptC: Start topical calcineurin inhibitors (EG: tacrolimus, pimecrolimus)
highlight_terms_source: topical corticosteroids and emollients with minimal improvement
why_right: The child has eczema with "minimal improvement" on topical corticosteroids and emollients. The next step on the eczema ladder is a steroid-sparing topical agent, a topical calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus or pimecrolimus), which controls inflammation without skin atrophy and is useful on the face and flexures.
why_wrong_block:
A. Elimination diets are not recommended routinely; they are used only when a specific food allergy is proven or strongly suspected to trigger flares.
B. Systemic corticosteroids cause rebound flares and long-term adverse effects in children; they are avoided except for short courses in severe flares under specialist care.
key_concept:
Eczema ladder: emollients + trigger avoidance → topical steroid → topical calcineurin inhibitor → phototherapy or systemic agents (specialist).
  • Check adherence and steroid phobia before escalating
  • Calcineurin inhibitors: steroid sparing, no skin atrophy, good for face and flexures
  • Infected eczema: treat the infection
  • Refractory severe disease: refer to dermatology
exam_pearl: If an option asks about compliance or parental concerns, that comes before escalating therapy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot; option C highlighted in pink; compiler line: 'Answer: C, Calcineurin Inhibitors'.

stem: A child present with 6 adenotonsillitis after starting kindergarten. mother reports snoring and mouth breathing. On examination there is grade 3 tonsils. What is the next step in management? No Mention Of Daytime Symptoms
why_right: The child has recurrent adenotonsillitis (6 episodes) plus snoring and mouth breathing with grade 3 tonsils, i.e. obstructive sleep disordered breathing from adenotonsillar hypertrophy. In an otherwise healthy child whose large tonsils match the snoring history, clinical diagnosis is enough and the next step is referral for adenotonsillectomy, which treats both problems. The note "no mention of daytime symptoms" signals there is no discordance that would require a sleep study first.
why_wrong_block: B. Polysomnography is the diagnostic test for OSA, but before pediatric tonsillectomy it is reserved for children with comorbidities (obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial or neuromuscular disease, sickle cell disease) or when tonsil size does not match the reported symptoms.
key_concept:
Child with snoring plus tonsillar hypertrophy: adenotonsillectomy is first line treatment.
  • Sleep study first: obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial anomaly, neuromuscular disease, sickle cell disease
  • Sleep study first: small tonsils but significant symptoms (discordance)
  • Recurrent tonsillitis threshold (Paradise): ≥7 in 1 year, ≥5 per year for 2 years, ≥3 per year for 3 years
  • Fewer episodes and no obstruction: watchful waiting
exam_pearl: Adult with daytime sleepiness and snoring: sleep study; healthy child with big tonsils and snoring: refer for adenotonsillectomy.

stem: A 2-year-old girl with fever and dysuria; treated for urinary tract infection 6 months ago. How to reduce risk of recurrent UTIs?
why_right: In a toddler with a recurrent UTI ("treated 6 months ago"), the most effective modifiable factor is bladder and bowel dysfunction: constipation compresses the bladder, causes incomplete emptying and urinary stasis. Treating and preventing constipation and establishing regular toilet habits (timed voiding, complete emptying) is the first line preventive measure and is favoured over hygiene advice alone or routine antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fruit juice (including cranberry) has weak evidence for preventing UTI in children and is not a recommended preventive strategy.
B. Long-term prophylaxis is not routine after one febrile UTI; it is reserved for selected children (e.g. high-grade VUR, frequent recurrences) given resistance and side effects.
C. Front to back perianal hygiene is reasonable advice, but when toilet training and constipation prevention is offered, it addresses the stronger risk factor (bladder and bowel dysfunction).
key_concept:
Recurrent pediatric UTI: fix the reversible risk factors first.
  • Constipation and incomplete bladder emptying: treat and prevent
  • Regular, timed voiding once toilet trained
  • Hygiene: front to back wiping in girls
  • Look for anatomy (VUR, posterior urethral valves) with imaging per guideline
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis: selected cases only
exam_pearl: When "constipation" appears among UTI prevention options, it wins over hygiene and over routine prophylaxis.

stem: A 2-year-old girl with fever and dysuria; treated for urinary tract infection 6 months ago. How to reduce risk of recurrent UTIs?
why_right: Same stem as the version with a constipation option, but here that option is absent. Among the remaining choices, proper perianal cleaning and hygiene (front to back wiping in a 2-year-old girl) is the simple, non-harmful preventive measure that reduces fecal flora reaching the short female urethra. It is the best available answer for preventing recurrence after a single prior UTI.
why_wrong_block:
A. Increasing fruit juice (cranberry) has no solid evidence of preventing UTI in young children and is not recommended.
B. Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis is not routine after one UTI 6 months ago; it is kept for selected high-risk children (e.g. high-grade VUR or frequent recurrences) because of resistance and adverse effects.
key_concept:
Preventing recurrent UTI in young girls: simple measures before antibiotics.
  • If offered: treat/prevent constipation and toilet habits (best)
  • Otherwise: perianal hygiene, front to back wiping
  • Adequate fluids, avoid holding urine
  • Prophylaxis: selected cases only
exam_pearl: Check the option list: if "toilet training and preventing constipation" is present, that is the key; without it, hygiene is chosen.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same stem as 734 but without the toilet-training option; here C is highlighted.

stem: Child complaining of nasal purulent discharge, eye pain, periorbital swelling and severe headache. On examination there is frontal bone tenderness and restricted extraocular movements. What is the most appropriate?
OptD: Refer to ear, nose, and throat (ENT)
why_right: Sinusitis (purulent discharge, frontal tenderness) with periorbital swelling, eye pain and restricted extraocular movements means the infection has spread behind the septum: orbital cellulitis, a complication. Restricted, painful eye movement separates it from preseptal cellulitis. Severe headache also raises concern for intracranial spread. A contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits, sinuses (and brain if needed) is required urgently to look for a subperiosteal or orbital abscess, alongside IV antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral amoxicillin treats uncomplicated acute bacterial sinusitis; orbital involvement needs admission, IV antibiotics and imaging.
C. Reassurance is never appropriate with eye signs; orbital cellulitis can cause vision loss, cavernous sinus thrombosis or brain abscess.
D. ENT (and ophthalmology) input is needed, but the CT is what defines an abscess needing drainage and should not be delayed; referral alone is not the most appropriate step.
key_concept:
Sinusitis with eye signs = complication until proven otherwise: contrast CT plus IV antibiotics.
  • Preseptal: lid swelling, normal eye movement, no proptosis, normal vision
  • Orbital: proptosis, painful restricted EOM, reduced acuity or colour vision, RAPD
  • Orbital spread usually from ethmoid sinusitis
  • Abscess on CT or worsening vision: surgical drainage
  • Severe headache or neuro signs: include brain imaging
exam_pearl: Restricted or painful eye movement is the single sign that turns preseptal (oral antibiotics) into orbital cellulitis (CT and IV antibiotics).

stem: child with a history of egg allergy is scheduled to receive the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine and the influenza vaccine. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine and the influenza vaccine
why_right: Egg allergy is not a contraindication to either vaccine. MMR is grown in chick embryo fibroblast culture and contains negligible egg protein, so it is given routinely even to egg allergic children. Current guidance also allows inactivated influenza vaccine in egg allergic children, with the usual post-vaccination observation; so the child receives both. (A repeated version keys this as "give both and observe".)
why_wrong_block:
B. Withholding influenza vaccine for egg allergy is outdated; egg allergy (even beyond hives) does not contraindicate inactivated influenza vaccine.
C. Withholding MMR is wrong: egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR. MMR is withheld for anaphylaxis to gelatin or neomycin, pregnancy or significant immunosuppression.
D. Deferring both leaves the child unprotected for no valid reason; the true absolute contraindication is anaphylaxis to a previous dose or to a vaccine component.
key_concept:
Egg allergy and vaccines:
  • MMR: give (chick fibroblast culture, not egg)
  • Inactivated influenza: give, with routine observation
  • Yellow fever: contains egg protein, needs allergist assessment
  • MMR/varicella true issue: gelatin or neomycin anaphylaxis
  • Absolute contraindication to any vaccine: anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component
exam_pearl: The only egg-related vaccine to stop and refer for is yellow fever; MMR and flu go ahead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Repeated (Q:) version with options reordered: A) Give MMR but not influenza, B) Give both and observe [highlighted], C) Give influenza but not MMR, D) Do not give either vaccine.

stem: Newborn of diabetic mother with jittery movements. What to check for?
why_right: An infant of a diabetic mother has fetal hyperinsulinism from chronic exposure to maternal hyperglycemia; after cord clamping the glucose supply stops but insulin stays high, causing neonatal hypoglycemia in the first hours of life. Jitteriness is a common presenting sign, and hypoglycemia is the most frequent and most dangerous (brain injury) cause, so blood glucose is checked first.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sodium disturbance is not a characteristic metabolic problem of infants of diabetic mothers and is an uncommon cause of jitteriness.
B. Hypocalcemia does occur in infants of diabetic mothers and can cause jitteriness, but it is less common and usually later than hypoglycemia; check calcium if glucose is normal.
C. Hypomagnesemia also occurs (and accompanies hypocalcemia), but it is a secondary consideration after glucose and calcium.
key_concept:
Infant of diabetic mother: problems to anticipate.
  • Hypoglycemia (most common, first hours): check glucose first
  • Hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia
  • Polycythemia, hyperbilirubinemia
  • Macrosomia, birth trauma, RDS
  • Congenital anomalies (cardiac, caudal regression)
exam_pearl: Jittery newborn of any kind: bedside glucose first; then calcium and magnesium.

stem: 4 month old infant previously had kernicterus with neurological sequelae. What is the expected finding in examination?
why_right: Kernicterus is deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia (globus pallidus) and brainstem nuclei. Basal ganglia damage produces dyskinetic (athetoid) cerebral palsy with involuntary writhing movements and dystonia, so the neurological sequelae expected on motor examination are dyskinetic.
why_wrong_block:
A. Spastic CP is from upper motor neuron damage (periventricular white matter or cortex), classically with prematurity or HIE, not bilirubin injury of the basal ganglia.
C. Hypotonia can be seen early in bilirubin encephalopathy, but it is nonspecific and evolves; the characteristic chronic sequela is dyskinetic movement.
D. Ataxic CP results from cerebellar damage, not basal ganglia injury.
key_concept:
CP type by lesion site:
  • Spastic: pyramidal tract/white matter (prematurity, PVL)
  • Dyskinetic/athetoid: basal ganglia (kernicterus, HIE)
  • Ataxic: cerebellum
  • Chronic kernicterus tetrad: athetosis, upward gaze palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, dental enamel dysplasia
exam_pearl: Kernicterus to basal ganglia to dyskinetic (athetoid) CP; do not be pulled by "spastic", the most common CP overall.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): A baby (No Age) with kernicterus and has neurological sequelae. What you will expect on his motor examination? A. Spasticity, B. Ataxia, C. Hypotonia, D. Dyskinesia [highlighted].

stem: A child with symptoms suggestive of functional constipation. Which of the following supports the diagnosis?
OptB: Sacral dimple and loss of anal tone
OptC: Normal intake and two stools per day
why_right: Functional constipation in children is defined clinically by infrequent (≤2 per week), hard or painful stools with withholding, large stools and fecal incontinence (soiling) from overflow around a retained mass. "Infrequent hard stool with soiling" combines these core features and supports a functional diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. A sacral dimple with loss of anal tone is a red flag for spinal dysraphism or tethered cord (organic, neurogenic bowel), arguing against functional constipation and needing spinal imaging.
C. Normal intake with two stools a day is a normal bowel pattern and does not support constipation at all.
key_concept:
Pediatric functional constipation (clinical diagnosis, no tests needed):
  • ≤2 stools per week, hard or painful stools
  • Withholding behaviour, large diameter stools
  • Fecal incontinence/soiling (overflow)
  • Red flags for organic cause: delayed meconium, failure to thrive, abnormal spine or anal tone, ribbon stools, bilious vomiting
exam_pearl: Soiling in a constipated child is overflow, a feature of functional constipation, not a sign of diarrhea.

stem: A patient presented after a road-traffic accident with severe injuries. He was unconscious with a GCS of 6. Examination revealed significant instability as well as multiple fractures and other injuries. The patient was hypotensive and tachycardic. What is the Most Appropriate management?
why_right: After an RTA he is hypotensive and tachycardic with an unstable pelvis ("significant instability") and multiple fractures. An unstable pelvic ring bleeding into the pelvis is the likely source of shock.
